meta.blurb: A hand touches Walter Hartright's arm on a dark road at midnight. It belongs to a woman dressed all in white, and she is running from someone. Soon a smiling count with pet white mice begins to plan something terrible.
meta.bible: Walter Hartright: a young drawing master and the hero; honest, brave, in love with Laura. The woman in white: Anne Catherick, a frail, frightened woman who escapes from an asylum and looks very like Laura; weak heart. Laura Fairlie: gentle, fair-haired heiress; becomes Lady Glyde; Mr Fairlie's niece. Marian Halcombe: Laura's half-sister, plain-faced, brave and clever; keeps a diary. Mr Fairlie: Laura's selfish, nervous uncle, owner of Limmeridge House. Sir Percival Glyde: a baronet in debt, who marries Laura for her money; secretly not the rightful heir to his name. Count Fosco: a huge, charming, clever Italian with white mice and a pet canary; the real villain; a traitor to a secret society. Madame Fosco: the Count's silent wife, Laura's aunt. Pesca: Walter's cheerful Italian friend, a member of the secret Brotherhood; Walter once saved his life. Mr Gilmore: the family lawyer. Mr Kyrle: the London lawyer Walter consults. Mrs Catherick: Anne's proud mother, who lives in Southampton and knows Percival's secret. Mrs Fairlie: the late mother of Laura and Marian, who once taught Anne Catherick at the village school; buried at Limmeridge. Limmeridge House: the Fairlie home in Cumberland. Cumberland: the county. Blackwater Park: Sir Percival's gloomy house in Hampshire. Hampshire: the county. Welmingham: the village with the old church and its register. Southampton. London. Paris. Italy. Central America. The Brotherhood: a secret Italian society that punishes traitors. Voice and tone: a classic mystery told by several witnesses, with a rising sense of dread and then triumph; deaths are stated plainly, with no gore. The plot: Anne is dying and has Laura's face; the Count and Sir Percival swap them, so that Laura is shut up as Anne while Anne is buried as Laura; Walter, Marian and Laura prove the truth with a forged marriage register, a confession and a date. Louis: Mr Fairlie's valet. Mrs Hartright and Sarah Hartright: Walter's mother and sister, who live in Hampstead. Mrs Clements: Anne's kind old friend, who lives at Todd's Corner, a farm near Limmeridge. Mr Merriman: Sir Percival's lawyer. Mrs Michelson: the cold housekeeper of Blackwater Park. Mr Dawson: the doctor who treats Marian's fever. Hester Pinhorn: the Count's cook in St John's Wood, London. Mrs Rubelle: the nurse who takes Laura to the asylum. Mr Catherick: Mrs Catherick's husband, the old parish clerk of Welmingham, who kept the vestry key. Sir Felix Glyde: Sir Percival's father. St John's Wood: the part of London where the Count lives. Hampstead: where Walter's mother lives. Dates: Anne dies on the twenty-fifth of July in the Count's house; Laura reaches London on the twenty-sixth. The Count's pets: a family of white mice, a cockatoo and two canaries. The Count dies in Paris, killed by the Brotherhood; his arm bears their red mark. Walter's drawing of Laura is a keepsake.
chapters: The Lady Who Was Not Laura

beats.scene: Walter walks alone down a moonlit road toward London at midnight
beats.summary: After an evening with his mother and sister, Walter Hartright walks home alone at midnight.

beats.scene: A hand touches Walter's shoulder; a woman in white stands behind him
beats.summary: A hand touches Walter's shoulder, and he turns to see a woman dressed all in white.

beats.scene: The woman in white asks Walter the way to London
beats.summary: The stranger asks the way to London and begs Walter not to question her.

beats.scene: Walter and the woman walk side by side along the empty road
beats.summary: They walk toward the city, and the woman is nervous at every sound.

beats.scene: The woman asks Walter if he knows a baronet named Sir Percival Glyde
beats.summary: She asks whether Walter knows any gentleman of rank, and asks about Sir Percival Glyde.

beats.scene: The woman in white speaks warmly of Mrs Fairlie and Limmeridge in Cumberland
beats.summary: The woman says that she was once happy in Cumberland, where a Mrs Fairlie was kind to her.

beats.scene: Walter calls a cab at the edge of London and helps the woman inside
beats.summary: At the edge of the town Walter finds a cab, and the woman gets in, thanking him.

beats.scene: A carriage stops, and a man asks a policeman about a woman in white
beats.summary: A carriage stops beside Walter, and men ask a policeman about a woman in white.

beats.scene: The men tell Walter that the woman has escaped from an asylum
beats.summary: The men tell Walter that she has escaped from an asylum, and he is ashamed to have helped her.

beats.scene: Walter lies awake at night thinking of the woman's face
beats.summary: Walter goes home troubled, and cannot decide whether she was wronged or ill.

beats.scene: Small, excited Pesca hurries into Walter's room with news
beats.summary: Walter's friend Pesca, the cheerful Italian professor, comes to see him with exciting news.

beats.scene: Pesca explains the offer of work from Mr Fairlie of Limmeridge House
beats.summary: Pesca says that a Mr Fairlie of Limmeridge House needs a drawing master, and Walter is startled by the name.

beats.scene: Walter tells his mother and sister about the offer and the woman in white
beats.summary: Walter tells his mother and his sister Sarah about the job and the strange night, and his mother is uneasy.

beats.scene: Pesca kisses Walter on both cheeks at the station as the train leaves
beats.summary: Pesca, who left his own country for reasons he never explains, sees Walter off at the station.

beats.scene: A train runs north through green fields toward Cumberland
beats.summary: Walter travels north by train and coach to the far country of Cumberland.

beats.scene: Limmeridge House stands large and grey in the evening light
beats.summary: Walter reaches the old grey house of Limmeridge at dusk.

beats.scene: Marian Halcombe stands by a window; Walter sees her figure and then her face
beats.summary: Walter meets Marian Halcombe, whose figure is beautiful and whose face is plain, but whose eyes are kind and quick.

beats.scene: Marian describes the household and Mr Fairlie's nerves over a late supper
beats.summary: Over supper Marian explains that her half-sister Laura has a headache and that Mr Fairlie suffers from his nerves.

beats.scene: Marian tells Walter his duties and speaks frankly about herself
beats.summary: Marian says what Walter must do, and says plainly that she is the plain sister and Laura is the beauty.

beats.scene: Walter looks from his bedroom window at the hills under the moon
beats.summary: Alone in his room, Walter looks out at the moonlit hills and thinks again of the woman in white.

beats.scene: Mr Fairlie, wrapped in a shawl, sits among his rare coins and prints
beats.summary: Walter meets Mr Fairlie, a pale, selfish invalid who lives among his coins and prints and hates noise.

beats.scene: Mr Fairlie gives weary orders from his chair and begs for quiet
beats.summary: Mr Fairlie says what he wants done and begs Walter to speak softly and not to bother him.

beats.scene: Walter sorts a heap of old drawings in a bright room with tall windows
beats.summary: Walter sets to work among a great heap of drawings in a bright room, and is happy with it.

beats.scene: Laura Fairlie sits at the piano in the sunny drawing room, fair and shy
beats.summary: Walter meets Laura Fairlie, a slender fair-haired girl with soft blue eyes, who is playing the piano.

beats.scene: Walter teaches Marian and Laura to sketch around a table of paints
beats.summary: The lessons begin, and Walter finds Marian quick and Laura gentle and patient.

beats.scene: Walter and Laura sketch on the moor while Marian reads in the sun
beats.summary: In the fine weather the lessons move outdoors, and Laura talks to Walter about her childhood and her father.

beats.scene: Laura plays the piano in the evening while Walter and Marian listen
beats.summary: In the evenings Laura plays and Walter listens, with Marian watching them from her chair.

beats.scene: Walter admits to himself that he loves Laura and that it is hopeless
beats.summary: Walter realises that he has fallen in love with Laura and knows that it can come to nothing.

beats.scene: Walter tells a story at the fireside while Laura listens and Marian turns pale
beats.summary: One evening Walter tells the story of the woman in white, and Marian grows pale at the name of Limmeridge.

beats.scene: Marian says that Mrs Fairlie once taught a girl named Anne Catherick
beats.summary: Marian says that Mrs Fairlie once had a pupil named Anne Catherick, who was always dressed in white, and goes to search the old letters.

beats.scene: Marian searches through a box of old letters by candlelight
beats.summary: Marian reads her mother's old letters and learns more about Anne Catherick and her mother.

beats.scene: Marian and Walter compare Laura's face with a memory of the woman in white
beats.summary: Marian and Walter agree that the woman in white must be Anne Catherick, and Marian notes a strange likeness to Laura.

beats.scene: Laura reads a letter at the breakfast table and turns white
beats.summary: A letter in an unknown hand arrives for Laura at breakfast; it warns her not to marry Sir Percival Glyde.

beats.scene: Marian tells Walter that Laura is engaged to Sir Percival
beats.summary: Walter learns that Laura is promised to Sir Percival, and that she gave her word to her dying father.

beats.scene: Walter searches the churchyard and the lanes for the writer of the letter
beats.summary: Marian and Walter agree that Anne herself wrote the letter, and Walter looks for her around Limmeridge.

beats.scene: Anne Catherick kneels at the white marble tomb of Mrs Fairlie in the dusk
beats.summary: At dusk Walter finds the woman in white beside Mrs Fairlie's white tomb and sees how like Laura she is.

beats.scene: Anne tells Walter, beside the tomb, about a dangerous secret
beats.summary: Anne tells Walter that she wrote the letter, and that Sir Percival shut her in an asylum because she knows his secret.

beats.scene: Anne sees Marian coming and runs away across the fields; Walter calls after her
beats.summary: Anne sees someone coming and runs away, and Walter follows her track to a farm called Todd's Corner, where he finds a kind woman, Mrs Clements.

beats.scene: Marian tells Walter, kindly and firmly, that he must leave Limmeridge
beats.summary: Marian says that Walter must go, for Laura's sake, and he agrees.

beats.scene: Laura gives Walter a small drawing in the garden and says goodbye
beats.summary: Laura gives Walter a small drawing and says that she must keep her promise; he leaves Limmeridge, and sails for Central America.

beats.scene: An old lawyer, Mr Gilmore, steps down from a carriage at Limmeridge House
beats.summary: Mr Gilmore, the old family lawyer, arrives at Limmeridge to prepare Laura's marriage papers.

beats.scene: Mr Gilmore speaks with Laura in the library; she is pale and quiet
beats.summary: Mr Gilmore finds Laura pale and sad, and she tells him that she will keep her word.

beats.scene: Marian hands Mr Gilmore the strange letter that warned Laura
beats.summary: Marian shows Mr Gilmore the anonymous letter, and he writes to Sir Percival's lawyer, Mr Merriman.

beats.scene: Sir Percival's letter explains that Anne Catherick is a poor sick woman
beats.summary: Sir Percival replies that Anne Catherick is a poor, sick woman, whom he put in an asylum at her mother's wish.

beats.scene: Sir Percival Glyde arrives at Limmeridge, polite and quick, and bows to Laura
beats.summary: Sir Percival arrives at Limmeridge, polite and quick of speech, and Laura greets him coldly.

beats.scene: Mr Gilmore and Mr Merriman argue over the settlement of Laura's money
beats.summary: Mr Gilmore wants Laura's fortune protected for her family, but Sir Percival's lawyer argues that it should go to Sir Percival.

beats.scene: Mr Fairlie waves a thin hand and refuses to be troubled about the money
beats.summary: Mr Fairlie refuses to help; Mr Gilmore gives way, and the money would pass to Sir Percival if Laura died.

beats.scene: Mr Gilmore says goodbye to Marian at the door of the house
beats.summary: Mr Gilmore leaves Limmeridge uneasy, and Marian promises herself to watch over Laura.

beats.scene: Laura in white marries Sir Percival in the village church
beats.summary: In December Laura marries Sir Percival in the village church, with Marian at her side.

beats.scene: A carriage drives away while Marian waves from the steps
beats.summary: The couple leave for six months in Italy, and Marian stays behind at Limmeridge.

beats.scene: Marian reads a short letter at the breakfast table with a worried frown
beats.summary: Laura's letters from Italy are short and cold, and Marian worries about her.

beats.scene: Marian meets the returning couple in the hall of Blackwater Park in June
beats.summary: In June the couple return, and Marian goes to join them at Blackwater Park and finds Laura changed.

beats.scene: A gloomy old house stands behind tall dark trees beside a still lake
beats.summary: Marian describes Blackwater Park: a gloomy old house with a dark lake, a boathouse and a closed wing.

beats.scene: Mrs Michelson, the housekeeper, stands stiffly in the hall; Sir Percival frowns
beats.summary: Marian meets the cold housekeeper, Mrs Michelson, and sees that Sir Percival is quick to anger.

beats.scene: Marian sits on Laura's bed at night, holding her hand by candlelight
beats.summary: At night Laura admits to Marian that she is not happy, and Marian promises not to leave her.

beats.scene: Sir Percival reads a letter and announces that guests are coming to stay
beats.summary: Sir Percival announces that his friend Count Fosco and the Count's wife, Laura's aunt, are coming to stay.

beats.scene: Madame Fosco steps from the carriage in a plain dress, silent and stiff
beats.summary: Madame Fosco arrives, and she is quiet, stiff and wonderfully changed from the talkative woman Marian remembered.

beats.scene: Count Fosco, enormous and smiling, steps down with a cage of white mice
beats.summary: Count Fosco arrives, huge, soft-spoken and smiling, with his birds and his white mice.

beats.scene: The Count kisses Laura's hand and bows to Marian in the hall
beats.summary: The Count charms them all with his kind manners, and Marian feels both drawn to him and afraid.

beats.scene: At the first dinner the Count tells stories while Sir Percival sits silent
beats.summary: At dinner the Count entertains everyone, and that night Marian writes in her diary that she fears him.

beats.scene: White mice run up the Count's sleeve while he talks to them softly
beats.summary: The Count trains his white mice, lets them run on his hands and sleeves, and talks to them like children.

beats.scene: The Count feeds sugar to his cockatoo beside the canaries
beats.summary: The Count keeps a cockatoo and canaries, loves sweet things, makes his own tea and sings opera.

beats.scene: Marian talks with the Count on the terrace while he strokes a mouse
beats.summary: Marian is drawn into conversation with the Count and admits that he is clever, amusing and well informed.

beats.scene: The Count calms Sir Percival with a few quiet words while Madame Fosco watches
beats.summary: Marian sees that Sir Percival obeys the Count, and that Madame Fosco watches everything.

beats.scene: Strange men at the door ask for Sir Percival
beats.summary: Strange callers come to the door asking for Sir Percival, and Marian learns that he is in debt.

beats.scene: Sir Percival tells Laura that she must sign a paper he cannot explain
beats.summary: Sir Percival tells Laura that he needs her to sign a paper to raise money, but will not say what it contains.

beats.scene: The Count and Madame Fosco stand beside Sir Percival, who holds a folded paper
beats.summary: In the library Sir Percival holds out a paper folded to hide its words, with the Count and his wife standing as witnesses.

beats.scene: Laura stands firm while Sir Percival strikes the table
beats.summary: Laura refuses to sign without reading the paper, and Sir Percival loses his temper and strikes the table.

beats.scene: The Count steps between them and quiets the room with a raised hand
beats.summary: The Count says the paper can wait, and Sir Percival storms out of the room.

beats.scene: Marian writes a letter at a small desk while the Count's mice squeak nearby
beats.summary: Marian writes to Mr Fairlie, asking him to invite Laura home, and he refuses, saying he cannot bear any trouble.

beats.scene: Sir Percival bows to Laura at breakfast while Marian watches him doubtfully
beats.summary: Sir Percival apologises the next day and is cheerful, but Marian does not trust him.

beats.scene: A farm boy gives Laura a folded note in the garden
beats.summary: A farm boy brings Laura a note: Anne Catherick is nearby and begs to meet her at the old boathouse.

beats.scene: Marian waits among the fir trees while Laura walks toward the boathouse
beats.summary: Marian warns Laura to take care, and Laura goes, while Marian waits among the trees.

beats.scene: Anne Catherick, in white, waits inside the dim boathouse; Laura stands before her
beats.summary: Laura meets Anne in the boathouse, and the likeness between the two women is startling.

beats.scene: Anne whispers about Sir Percival's secret and her mother's part in it
beats.summary: Anne says that Sir Percival's secret is so great that it could ruin him, and that her mother knows it too.

beats.scene: Anne whispers an offer to Laura inside the dim boathouse
beats.summary: Anne offers to tell Laura the secret, but Laura will not promise to hide it from her sister.

beats.scene: A shadow falls across the wall of the boathouse and Anne springs up
beats.summary: A shadow falls across the boathouse wall, and Anne runs away into the woods, saying that someone has watched them.

beats.scene: Sir Percival grips Laura by the arm in the hall
beats.summary: Sir Percival learns of the meeting from Madame Fosco and seizes Laura's arm, demanding to know what Anne said.

beats.scene: Marian pulls Sir Percival's hand away while the Count enters the hall
beats.summary: Marian steps between them, and the Count enters and calms Sir Percival once again.

beats.scene: Men with lanterns search the dark fields and woods around the lake
beats.summary: Sir Percival sends men to search for Anne, but she has vanished, and Marian decides to find out their plans.

beats.scene: Marian climbs out onto the low veranda roof at night
beats.summary: On a close, thundery night Marian sees a light below and climbs out onto the roof of the veranda to listen.

beats.scene: Two men talk on a dark terrace below Marian's hiding place
beats.summary: Marian hears Sir Percival tell the Count that he is in terrible need of money and that his creditors will not wait.

beats.scene: The Count speaks calmly to Sir Percival, who says there must be no violence
beats.summary: The Count says that Laura's money can be had by other means, and Sir Percival says that there must be no violence.

beats.scene: Marian strains to hear the men's low voices as the wind rises
beats.summary: The men speak of Anne Catherick and of how like Laura she is, but the wind rises, and Marian can hear no more.

beats.scene: Rain pours down on Marian as she clings to the roof, soaked and shivering
beats.summary: A thunderstorm breaks, and Marian lies on the roof for hours in the pouring rain.

beats.scene: Marian crawls back through her window and drops to the floor, wet and cold
beats.summary: At last Marian crawls back through her window, soaked and chilled to the bone, and falls shivering onto the floor.

beats.scene: Marian writes in her diary with a shaking hand by a single candle
beats.summary: With a shaking hand Marian writes down all that she has heard, and warns herself to protect Laura.

beats.scene: Laura finds Marian burning with fever on her bed in the morning
beats.summary: In the morning Laura finds Marian in a high fever, and Mr Dawson the doctor is sent for.

beats.scene: Mr Dawson shakes his head over Marian's bed while the Count offers help
beats.summary: Mr Dawson says that the fever is serious, and the Count and his wife kindly offer to help with the nursing.

beats.scene: Laura sits beside the bed night after night while the house falls quiet
beats.summary: For many nights Laura nurses Marian, who lies delirious, while the great house falls quiet around them.

beats.scene: The Count tiptoes in and draws a book from under Marian's pillow
beats.summary: While Marian lies ill, the Count steps into her room at night and finds her diary under her pillow.

beats.scene: The Count reads the diary by candlelight, nodding and smiling at every page
beats.summary: The Count reads every page of the diary and learns all that Marian knows and all that she suspects.

beats.scene: The Count writes a note in bold handwriting at the diary's end
beats.summary: The Count writes a polite note in the diary, praising Marian and telling her that he admires her courage.

beats.scene: Sir Percival sends away the servants and Mrs Michelson prepares to leave
beats.summary: Sir Percival suddenly dismisses most of the servants, and Mrs Michelson is sent to the seaside, so the house is almost empty.

beats.scene: Laura begs at a sickroom door while the Count shakes his head
beats.summary: Laura begs to sit with Marian, but is told that the sickroom is dangerous, and her letter to Mr Fairlie is never sent.

beats.scene: Marian wakes weak and pale, finds her diary, and reads the Count's note
beats.summary: Marian wakes at last, weak but clear in her mind, and finds the Count's note in her diary.

beats.scene: Mr Dawson speaks with the Count, who suggests that Marian should go north
beats.summary: Mr Dawson says that Marian is better, and the Count suggests that she should go to Limmeridge to recover.

beats.scene: Marian is helped into a carriage while Laura waves from a window above
beats.summary: Marian, still very weak, is helped into a carriage and sent north, and she sees Laura at the window.

beats.scene: The Count tells Laura that Marian has stopped in London and waits for her
beats.summary: The Count and Sir Percival tell Laura that Marian had to rest in London and wants her to come.

beats.scene: Laura looks out of a train window as the green fields run past
beats.summary: Laura leaves Blackwater Park alone by train, hoping to find her sister at the end of the journey.

beats.scene: Anne Catherick, ill and pale, rests in a plain London room beside Mrs Clements
beats.summary: Meanwhile in London Anne Catherick is ill and frightened, with her heart growing weaker.

beats.scene: Madame Fosco leads a weak, shawled Anne into a tall house
beats.summary: Madame Fosco finds Anne, and she is taken to the Count's London house in St John's Wood.

beats.scene: A doctor writes at a small table beside the bed where Anne lies still
beats.summary: Anne dies of her weak heart on the twenty-fifth of July, and the doctor writes a certificate in the name of Lady Glyde.

beats.scene: The Count meets Laura at the London station, bowing with a smile
beats.summary: The next day Laura arrives in London, and the Count meets her at the station with a smile.

beats.scene: The cab rolls through London streets toward a tall house with green shutters
beats.summary: The Count takes Laura to his house, where Marian is not to be found, and Madame Fosco says that she is out.

beats.scene: Madame Fosco pours a cup of tea; Laura sips it and grows faint
beats.summary: Madame Fosco gives Laura a cup of tea that tastes strange, and Laura feels faint and falls.

beats.scene: Laura wakes in a bare room in a strange dress marked with Anne's name
beats.summary: Laura wakes in a bare room, dressed in Anne's clothes, and is told that she is Anne Catherick, an escaped patient.

beats.scene: A closed carriage waits at the door; Laura is led out between two women
beats.summary: Laura is driven away in a closed carriage, protesting, and nobody believes her.

beats.scene: A heavy asylum door opens for a pale woman in plain dress
beats.summary: At the asylum gate the doctor accepts Laura as Anne Catherick, and he smiles at her claim to be Lady Glyde.

beats.scene: Laura sits in a bare room with high barred windows
beats.summary: Laura lives in the asylum among strangers, treated kindly but firmly, while her protests are called signs of illness.

beats.scene: A black-edged letter lies on the table beside Mr Fairlie's breakfast tray
beats.summary: A letter reaches Limmeridge saying that Lady Glyde has died in London of heart disease.

beats.scene: Marian stands pale and still at the window while Mr Fairlie weeps loudly
beats.summary: Marian is struck with grief and horror, while Mr Fairlie complains of how much the news has upset his nerves.

beats.scene: A hearse rolls slowly up the village road behind four black horses
beats.summary: Sir Percival arranges for the coffin to be buried at Limmeridge, and it travels north by road.

beats.scene: Villagers in black stand around the open vault in the churchyard
beats.summary: The funeral takes place at Limmeridge, and the tomb is marked with the name of Laura, Lady Glyde.

beats.scene: Marian lays a hand on the white marble and stares at the new name
beats.summary: Marian stays at the tomb after the others have left, and she cannot believe that Laura lies there.

beats.scene: Marian opens the diary by lamplight and reads the Count's long note again
beats.summary: Marian rereads the diary and the Count's note, and begins to see how carefully the Count has planned everything.

beats.scene: Mrs Clements arrives at Limmeridge asking for news of Anne
beats.summary: Mrs Clements arrives at Limmeridge in great distress, because Anne has vanished from London.

beats.scene: Marian understands that the woman buried as Laura may be Anne Catherick
beats.summary: Marian realises that Anne vanished just before Laura was said to have died, and suspects that the dead woman is Anne.

beats.scene: Marian packs a small bag and boards a train for London
beats.summary: Marian leaves Limmeridge for London to learn the truth, but the Count's house is empty and the Count has left.

beats.scene: Mrs Clements and Marian stand before the tall gate of a private asylum
beats.summary: Mrs Clements tells Marian where Anne was kept before, and Marian goes to that asylum to ask about a new patient.

beats.scene: The porter shakes his head at the gate while Marian argues
beats.summary: The porter refuses to answer Marian's questions, and the doctor will not let her in.

beats.scene: Marian presses coins into a nurse's hand beside a high wall
beats.summary: Marian waits near the gate and bribes a nurse, who tells her that a new patient has come, who insists that she is Lady Glyde.

beats.scene: Patients in white walk in a walled garden at dusk
beats.summary: The nurse arranges for Marian to watch from behind the wall as the patients take their evening walk in the garden.

beats.scene: Marian and Laura embrace in the dusk of the garden
beats.summary: Marian steps out and sees that the thin woman is Laura, who is almost too weak and dazed to know her.

beats.scene: Marian whispers a plan to the nurse beside a shadowed doorway
beats.summary: Marian pays the nurse to help Laura escape that very night, and promises that a cab will wait outside the gate.

beats.scene: Marian waits by a cab in a cold lane at midnight
beats.summary: At midnight Marian waits in the cold lane beside a cab, and every minute seems like an hour.

beats.scene: A small door opens in the wall and Laura stumbles out
beats.summary: At last the small door opens, and the nurse pushes Laura out into Marian's arms before closing it again.

beats.scene: Two women lift Laura into a cab and drive away
beats.summary: Marian and Mrs Clements lift Laura into the cab, and the driver whips up the horse and drives away into the night.

beats.scene: Laura sleeps in a narrow bed while Marian sits beside her
beats.summary: Laura sleeps for a day in Marian's lodgings, and when she wakes, she tells Marian about the tea and the asylum.

beats.scene: Marian counts her last few coins at a small table while Laura sleeps
beats.summary: Marian has little money and Laura's mind is still clouded, but Marian resolves that nobody shall ever take her sister away again.

beats.scene: A thin, sunburnt Walter stands at a ship's rail near England
beats.summary: After months of danger and fever in Central America, Walter comes home to England, thinner and older.

beats.scene: Walter's mother and sister embrace him in the doorway of their cottage
beats.summary: Walter hurries to his mother and sister, who greet him with joy, but they have sad news from Limmeridge.

beats.scene: Walter reads the new name on the white tomb in the Limmeridge churchyard
beats.summary: Walter travels to Limmeridge, to the churchyard, where he reads Laura's name on the white tomb.

beats.scene: Two women in thick veils walk through the churchyard gate toward the tomb
beats.summary: While Walter sits there, two women in thick veils come into the churchyard, and he steps behind a tree to avoid them.

beats.scene: One of the veiled women lifts her veil and shows Laura's living face
beats.summary: One of the women lifts her veil beside the tomb, and Walter sees Laura's face, alive.

beats.scene: Marian turns and recognises Walter; Laura stares at him with uncertain eyes
beats.summary: Marian cries out at the sight of Walter, and Laura looks at him slowly, as though she were remembering.

beats.scene: Marian tells Walter the story in low words among the gravestones
beats.summary: Marian tells Walter the whole terrible story, and he learns that the tomb holds Anne Catherick, not Laura.

beats.scene: Walter leads two veiled women up the steps of a lodging house
beats.summary: Walter brings Marian and Laura back to London and finds them poor, cheap rooms near his own.

beats.scene: Marian sews, Laura draws, and Walter works in a poor room
beats.summary: The three live quietly on very little money, Marian sewing, Laura drawing slowly, and Walter working long hours for pay.

beats.scene: Walter swears a promise before Laura and Marian in a bare room
beats.summary: Walter swears that he will give Laura back her name and make those who wronged her answer for it.

beats.scene: Walter faces Mr Kyrle across a desk heaped with papers
beats.summary: Walter goes to Mr Kyrle, a London lawyer, and tells him the whole story.

beats.scene: Mr Kyrle shakes his head over the papers and explains what the law requires
beats.summary: Mr Kyrle says that the law needs strong proof, and that the certificate, the funeral and the tomb all say that Laura is dead.

beats.scene: Mr Kyrle taps a calendar on his desk
beats.summary: Mr Kyrle says that the date of Lady Glyde's death is the weak point, and that if Laura was alive after it, the certificate must be false.

beats.scene: Walter asks Laura gently about the day she left Blackwater Park
beats.summary: Walter asks Laura about her journey to London, but her memory is still too clouded to give a clear answer.

beats.scene: Walter sits with Mrs Clements in her small kitchen as she dries her eyes
beats.summary: Walter visits Mrs Clements, who tells him how Anne grew ill and vanished in London.

beats.scene: Mrs Clements points out of a window to the south and speaks of Welmingham
beats.summary: Mrs Clements tells Walter that Anne often spoke of her mother in Welmingham, where Sir Percival's secret was said to be kept.

beats.scene: Walter talks to Hester Pinhorn, the Count's former cook, in a London kitchen
beats.summary: Walter finds the Count's former cook, Hester Pinhorn, who says that a sick lady died in the house on the twenty-fifth of July.

beats.scene: Walter counts the dates on a calendar and looks at Marian's diary
beats.summary: Walter sees that if Anne died on the twenty-fifth and Laura reached London on the twenty-sixth, the certificate must be false, but Mr Kyrle says more proof is still needed.

beats.scene: Marian and Walter agree that Sir Percival's secret is the key
beats.summary: Walter and Marian agree that they must find Sir Percival's secret, which Anne had hinted at, to force him to confess.

beats.scene: Laura gives Walter a small coin for luck as he takes a train south
beats.summary: Walter says goodbye to Laura and Marian and leaves for Hampshire to learn the secret of Welmingham church.

beats.scene: Walter walks up a quiet lane toward a grey stone church in Welmingham
beats.summary: Walter arrives in the quiet village of Welmingham in Hampshire and walks up to the old grey church.

beats.scene: An old wrinkled clerk leans on his stick at a church door
beats.summary: Walter meets the old parish clerk, a deaf and talkative man, who agrees to show him the church.

beats.scene: An old clerk unlocks a small door beside an iron cupboard of books
beats.summary: The clerk shows Walter the vestry, a small room with an iron press in which the old registers are kept.

beats.scene: Walter turns the heavy pages of an old church register
beats.summary: Walter asks for the book that records Sir Felix Glyde's marriage, and finds the entry among the others.

beats.scene: Walter holds a lamp close to a page of crowded handwriting
beats.summary: Walter notices that the ink and the writing of the entry look different from those around it, as if it had been squeezed in later.

beats.scene: Walter copies the entry carefully onto paper while the old clerk dozes
beats.summary: Walter copies the entry word for word, while the old clerk dozes in the sun, and begins to suspect that the entry was forged.

beats.scene: The old clerk chats as Walter folds a copied page
beats.summary: The clerk wakes and talks of Mr Catherick, who was clerk before him, and of Mrs Catherick, who left in disgrace.

beats.scene: Walter walks up a quiet street to a neat house in Southampton
beats.summary: Walter takes the train to Southampton and finds Mrs Catherick's neat little house in a quiet street.

beats.scene: Mrs Catherick sits upright in her tidy parlour and looks coldly at Walter
beats.summary: Mrs Catherick, a proud and stern woman, receives Walter coldly in her tidy parlour and says that Sir Percival has always been generous to her.

beats.scene: Mrs Catherick flushes with anger in her tidy parlour
beats.summary: When Walter presses her about Anne, Mrs Catherick loses her temper and lets slip that Sir Percival has no right to his name.

beats.scene: Mrs Catherick seals a hurried letter with a shaking hand
beats.summary: After Walter leaves, Mrs Catherick writes to Sir Percival to warn him that a stranger is asking about his name.

beats.scene: Walter and Pesca sit in a London room while Pesca waves two tickets
beats.summary: Back in London, Walter tells Marian what he has found, and Pesca invites him to the opera.

beats.scene: At the opera Pesca stares in horror at a huge man in a box
beats.summary: At the opera Pesca stares in horror at a huge, calm man in a box on the other side of the theatre.

beats.scene: Pesca whispers a secret to Walter in the corridor of the theatre
beats.summary: Pesca explains in a whisper that the man is a traitor to a secret Italian society, the Brotherhood, and that his own life is in danger.

beats.scene: The Count rises in his box and looks across the theatre straight at Pesca
beats.summary: The Count notices Pesca, rises from his seat and leaves, and Walter realises from Marian's description that this is Count Fosco.

beats.scene: Walter hurries back by night to Welmingham and hides near the old church
beats.summary: Walter fears that Sir Percival will try to destroy the register, and returns to Welmingham to watch the church.

beats.scene: Sir Percival unlocks the vestry door with a false key and lifts a lantern
beats.summary: Sir Percival arrives at the church at night, opens the vestry door with a key he has had made, and goes in with a lantern.

beats.scene: Sir Percival tears a page out as lantern flames creep toward papers
beats.summary: Sir Percival tears out the page of the register, and the lantern sets fire to the dry papers in the small room.

beats.scene: Villagers run toward the burning church with buckets while Walter pulls at the door
beats.summary: The villagers rush to the burning church, and Walter and the old clerk try to break down the door.

beats.scene: A coroner questions Walter in a village inn about the fire
beats.summary: Sir Percival dies in the fire, and the coroner decides that it was an accident, while Walter feels no triumph.

beats.scene: Walter climbs a narrow staircase to the Count's rented rooms
beats.summary: Walter learns where the Count is lodging and climbs the stairs to his rooms.

beats.scene: The Count rises from his great chair among his cages and bows to Walter
beats.summary: The Count receives Walter with perfect politeness among his birds and mice, and Walter says plainly what he knows.

beats.scene: Walter names Pesca and the Brotherhood, and the Count's smile fades
beats.summary: Walter says that Pesca has recognised the Count as a traitor to the Brotherhood, and the Count's calm face turns pale.

beats.scene: Walter and the Count face each other across a table of cages
beats.summary: Walter offers the Count a bargain: a full written confession, in return for a few hours to escape before the Brotherhood is told.

beats.scene: The Count writes at a large table by lamplight, a mouse on his shoulder
beats.summary: The Count writes through the night with a mouse on his shoulder, pausing only to sip his coffee.

beats.scene: Madame Fosco sits silent in a corner as the Count writes
beats.summary: Madame Fosco sits silent in a corner, never taking her eyes from her husband, and Walter feels sorry for her.

beats.scene: Walter reads the Count's pages one by one at a lamplit table
beats.summary: The confession describes how Anne's death was used to bury Laura's name, how Laura was lured to London and taken to the asylum.

beats.scene: Walter's finger rests on a date in the Count's writing
beats.summary: The confession gives the dates, and shows that Laura was alive on the twenty-sixth of July, a day after the certificate says that she died.

beats.scene: The Count signs the last page with a great flourish
beats.summary: The Count finishes, signs with a flourish, and hands over the pages with a polite bow.

beats.scene: Walter walks home through the early morning streets with the confession in his coat
beats.summary: Walter leaves with the confession and, true to his word, says nothing until the Count has gone.

beats.scene: Marian and Laura read the Count's pages at a small table by the window
beats.summary: Marian and Laura read the Count's confession, and Marian is moved to anger and to hope.

beats.scene: A steamer carries the Count and Madame Fosco across the sea to France
beats.summary: The Count and his wife leave England the same day, and Walter keeps his promise to say nothing for several hours.

beats.scene: Walter reads a newspaper paragraph about an unknown man found dead in Paris
beats.summary: Some weeks later Walter reads in a newspaper about an unknown man found dead in a street in Paris.

beats.scene: Walter looks at a huge, calm face laid out in the Paris morgue
beats.summary: In the Paris morgue Walter sees the Count's body, with a mark on the arm that Pesca had told him about; the Brotherhood had killed him.

beats.scene: Pesca sits with his hands over his face in Walter's room and says little
beats.summary: Walter tells Pesca what he saw, and Pesca asks him never to speak of the Brotherhood again.

beats.scene: Mr Kyrle reads the Count's confession twice and strikes the desk with his hand
beats.summary: Mr Kyrle reads the confession and says that it is strong, but he advises Walter to gather more witnesses.

beats.scene: Mrs Michelson and Hester Pinhorn sign statements in the lawyer's office
beats.summary: Walter gathers sworn statements from Mrs Michelson and Hester Pinhorn about the last days at Blackwater Park and the death in the Count's house.

beats.scene: Marian copies out the pages of her diary at a table in the lamplight
beats.summary: Marian copies out her diary, including the Count's note, to be kept as evidence of what was planned at Blackwater Park.

beats.scene: Mr Kyrle advises Walter to take Laura to Limmeridge to be recognised
beats.summary: Mr Kyrle advises Walter to take Laura to Limmeridge, since the people who have known her since childhood will not be fooled.

beats.scene: A train runs north through mist with three travellers and a box
beats.summary: The three travel north together by train with all their papers, and Laura is clearer in her mind than she has been for months.

beats.scene: Villagers gather around Laura in the lane at Limmeridge, some weeping and some laughing
beats.summary: At Limmeridge the villagers and tenants recognise Laura at once and gather around her with tears of joy.

beats.scene: The tenants cheer as Marian leads Laura up the steps of Limmeridge House
beats.summary: The tenants cheer Laura all the way to Limmeridge House, and Marian leads her up the steps and through the front door.

beats.scene: Mr Fairlie, wrapped in a shawl, stares at Laura and the papers
beats.summary: Mr Fairlie, in his shawl, first refuses to believe, but Walter lays out the proofs and the tenants' voices are heard from outside.

beats.scene: Mr Fairlie reluctantly signs a paper that declares Laura to be his niece
beats.summary: Mr Fairlie, defeated, signs a paper that accepts Laura as his niece, and complains of his nerves.

beats.scene: A mason cuts a new name into the white tomb
beats.summary: The false inscription is cut away, and Anne Catherick is remembered at last under her own name.

beats.scene: Walter and Laura marry in the village church, with Marian beside them
beats.summary: Walter and Laura marry in the village church at Limmeridge, with Marian standing beside them as witness.

beats.scene: A baby boy sleeps in a cradle while Walter and Laura smile at him
beats.summary: Walter and Laura have a son, and Marian loves the little boy as if he were her own.

beats.scene: An old man lies in a big bed while a small boy plays
beats.summary: When Mr Fairlie dies, Walter and Laura's little boy becomes the heir to Limmeridge.

beats.scene: Walter pauses on the moonlit road where he once met a woman
beats.summary: Years later Walter passes the spot on the road where he first met Anne, and remembers her with kindness.

beats.scene: Walter writes at his desk while Laura and the little boy play behind him
beats.summary: Walter ends the story he has written so that the truth about Laura may be known to everyone.

A1A2: Walter Hartright left his mother's house and walked toward London at midnight.
Suddenly, a hand touched his shoulder, and Walter turned around quickly.
She asked him the way to London in a low, trembling voice.
They walked on together, and she looked behind her at every sound.
She asked if he knew a rich man named Sir Percival Glyde.
She said that Mrs Fairlie, a kind lady, once gave her white dresses.
Near the city, Walter found a cab and helped her inside.
Then a carriage stopped, and a man asked about a woman in white.
They said she had escaped from an asylum, and Walter felt afraid.
That night, Walter lay awake and thought about the strange woman.
A few days later, his little Italian friend Pesca came with news.
Pesca said that a rich man in Cumberland needed a drawing teacher.
Walter told his mother and sister about the job and the woman.
Pesca came to the station and wished Walter good luck.
The train ran north all day, past fields and hills.
At evening, Walter reached Limmeridge House, a large grey house.
Miss Halcombe turned from the window and smiled at him warmly.
Miss Halcombe said that her uncle was often ill and liked quiet.
She told him his work: to mount drawings and to teach her.
That night, Walter looked out at the moon over the hills.
Mr Fairlie sat in a soft chair, wrapped in a warm blanket.
Mr Fairlie told Walter his work and asked him to be quiet.
Walter began his work among the drawings in a bright room.
Laura Fairlie was playing the piano when Walter first saw her.
The lessons began, and Marian learned fast, but Laura was shy.
They sketched outdoors, and Laura talked about her father.
In the evening, Laura played music, and Walter listened quietly.
Walter knew now that he loved Laura, but he was poor.
One evening, Walter told them the story of the woman in white.
Marian said Mrs Fairlie once taught a girl named Anne Catherick.
Marian read old letters and found the name of Anne Catherick.
Marian said that Anne's face was very like Laura's face.
A strange letter came for Laura, and she read it, shaking.
Then Walter learned that Laura must soon marry Sir Percival.
They thought Anne had written it, so Walter went to look.
At dusk, Walter found Anne at Mrs Fairlie's white tomb.
Anne said that Sir Percival had put her in an asylum.
Anne saw someone coming and ran away, and Walter followed.
Marian told Walter that he must go, and he agreed sadly.
Laura gave Walter a drawing, and he left Limmeridge sadly.
Mr Gilmore, the family lawyer, came to prepare the marriage papers.
Laura was pale and quiet, and she said she would keep her word.
Marian showed the lawyer the letter, and he wrote to Sir Percival's lawyer.
Sir Percival answered that Anne was ill and her mother wished it.
Sir Percival arrived, and he was polite, but Laura was cold.
Mr Gilmore argued with Sir Percival's lawyer about Laura's money.
Mr Fairlie would not help, and Mr Gilmore gave way at last.
Mr Gilmore left with a heavy heart, and Marian watched Laura.
In December, Laura married Sir Percival in the village church.
The couple left for Italy, and Marian stayed at Limmeridge.
Laura's letters from Italy were short, and Marian was worried.
In June, Marian went to Blackwater Park and found Laura changed.
Blackwater Park was a gloomy old house beside a dark lake.
The housekeeper, Mrs Michelson, was cold, and Sir Percival was often angry.
At night, Laura told Marian she was not happy, and Marian stayed.
Sir Percival said that Count Fosco and his wife would visit.
Madame Fosco arrived, and she was quiet and very different.
Count Fosco arrived, a huge man with a smile and white mice.
The Count was kind to everyone, but Marian felt afraid of him.
At dinner, the Count told stories, and Marian wrote her fears.
The Count loved his white mice and let them run on his arms.
He also kept birds, ate many sweets, and sang opera songs.
Marian talked with the Count and found him clever and kind.
The Count calmed Sir Percival with a few quiet words.
Strange men came to the door asking for Sir Percival.
Sir Percival told Laura that she must sign a paper soon.
In the library, Sir Percival held out a paper folded to hide the writing.
Laura refused to sign without reading it, and Sir Percival raged.
The Count said the paper could wait, and Sir Percival left.
Marian wrote to Mr Fairlie, but he refused to help.
The next day, Sir Percival said sorry, but Marian did not trust him.
A boy gave Laura a note, and it was from Anne Catherick.
Laura went to the old house by the lake, and Marian waited.
By the lake, Anne waited, and the two women looked alike.
Anne said that Sir Percival had a secret and her mother knew it.
Anne offered to tell the secret, but Laura would not promise silence.
Then Anne saw a shadow on the wall and ran away.
Sir Percival held Laura by the arm and demanded the truth.
Marian stepped between them, and the Count quieted Sir Percival.
Men searched for Anne, but she had gone, and Marian decided to listen.
One hot night, Marian heard voices and climbed out onto the roof.
She heard Sir Percival say he needed money very soon.
The Count said there was a way, and Sir Percival was afraid.
They spoke about Anne Catherick, but the wind rose.
Then the storm broke, and heavy rain fell on Marian.
At last Marian climbed back into her room, cold and wet.
She wrote in her diary late at night with a shaking hand.
In the morning, Laura found Marian ill, and the doctor came.
Mr Dawson said the fever was serious, and the Count offered help.
For many nights, Laura sat beside Marian while the house was quiet.
At night, the Count came into Marian's room and found her diary.
He read every page and learned all that Marian knew.
The Count wrote a polite note in the diary and put it back.
Sir Percival sent the servants away, and the house grew empty.
Laura asked to see Marian, but she was told to stay away.
Marian woke up weak and found the Count's note in her diary.
Mr Dawson said Marian was better, and the Count suggested a journey.
Marian left in a carriage, weak, and Laura waved from the window.
The Count told Laura that Marian was waiting for her in London.
Laura left Blackwater Park alone by train to find Marian.
Meanwhile, in London, Anne was ill, and her heart was weak.
Madame Fosco found Anne and took her to the Count's house.
Anne died in the night, and the doctor wrote Lady Glyde's name.
The next day, the Count met Laura at the London station.
They drove to the Count's house, but Marian was not there.
Laura drank the tea, and it tasted strange, and she felt faint.
Laura woke in a bare room and was told she was Anne.
A closed carriage took Laura away, and nobody believed her.
At the asylum, the doctor smiled at Laura's claim and wrote it down.
In the asylum, Laura sat among strangers and nobody listened.
A black-edged letter came to Limmeridge: Lady Glyde was dead.
Marian was shocked and sad, but Mr Fairlie thought only of himself.
Sir Percival sent the coffin north to be buried at Limmeridge.
The funeral was held at Limmeridge, and the villagers cried.
After the funeral, Marian stood at the tomb, but she doubted.
Marian read her diary again and began to see the Count's plan.
Mrs Clements came to Limmeridge and said that Anne had vanished.
Marian thought that the dead woman might really be Anne.
Marian went to London, but the Count's house was empty.
Mrs Clements knew the asylum, and Marian went there to ask.
The porter would not answer, and the doctor would not see her.
Marian paid a nurse, who said a new patient called herself Lady Glyde.
The nurse let Marian watch the patients walk in the garden.
Marian saw that the pale woman was Laura, and she cried.
Marian made a plan with the nurse to take Laura away that night.
At midnight, Marian waited in the cold lane beside a cab.
At last a door opened, and Laura came out into the lane.
They lifted Laura into the cab and drove away through the night.
Laura slept for a day, and then she told Marian everything.
Marian had little money, but she promised to protect Laura.
After many months, Walter sailed home, thin and brown from the sun.
Walter hurried home to his mother and sister, who had sad news.
Walter went to Limmeridge and read Laura's name on the tomb.
Two women in veils walked in, and Walter hid behind a tree.
One woman lifted her veil, and Walter saw Laura's living face.
Marian cried out at Walter, and Laura looked at him slowly.
Marian told Walter all, and he learned that Anne was in the tomb.
Walter took them back to London and found them cheap rooms.
They lived on very little: Marian sewed, Laura drew, Walter worked.
Walter promised to give Laura back her name and her rights.
Walter went to a London lawyer, Mr Kyrle, and told him everything.
Mr Kyrle said the law needed strong proof that Laura was alive.
Mr Kyrle said the date of the death was the weak point.
Walter asked Laura about her journey, but she could not remember.
Walter visited Mrs Clements, and she told him about Anne's last days.
Mrs Clements said that the secret was kept at Welmingham.
Walter found the Count's cook, who remembered the sick lady's death.
Walter saw that the death date and Laura's journey did not match.
They agreed to find Sir Percival's secret to make him confess.
Walter said goodbye and took the train south to Welmingham.
Walter reached Welmingham, a quiet village with an old grey church.
The old clerk of the church was deaf and talked a great deal.
The clerk showed Walter the small room where the old books were kept.
Walter asked for the book about Sir Felix and found the page.
Walter saw that the ink of the entry was different from the rest.
Walter copied the entry carefully while the clerk slept in the sun.
The old clerk spoke of Mr Catherick, who kept the key long ago.
Walter took a train to Southampton and found Mrs Catherick's house.
Mrs Catherick was cold and proud, and she praised Sir Percival.
Mrs Catherick grew angry and said Sir Percival had no right to his name.
Mrs Catherick wrote to Sir Percival to warn him about Walter.
In London, Pesca invited Walter to the opera, and Walter agreed.
At the opera, Pesca saw a fat man and turned very pale.
Pesca whispered that the fat man was a traitor to a secret society.
The Count saw Pesca and left, and Walter knew who he was.
Walter feared for the register and went back to watch the church.
Sir Percival came at night with a key and went into the church.
Sir Percival tore out the page, and the lantern started a fire.
The villagers ran to the church, and Walter tried to open the door.
Sir Percival died in the fire, and the coroner called it an accident.
Walter found where the Count lived and climbed the stairs.
The Count received Walter politely among his birds and mice.
Walter named Pesca and the Brotherhood, and the Count went pale.
Walter offered a bargain: a written account for a few hours.
All night, the Count wrote his story, with a mouse on his shoulder.
Madame Fosco sat silent and watched her husband all night long.
The Count's story told how Anne died and Laura was sent away.
The dates proved that Laura was alive after the certificate said.
The Count signed his name with a flourish and bowed politely.
Walter went home with the confession, and he kept his word.
Marian and Laura read the confession and felt angry and hopeful.
The Count and his wife left England, and Walter kept his word.
Weeks later, Walter read about a man found dead in Paris.
In Paris, Walter saw the Count dead, and he knew who had done it.
Walter told Pesca, and Pesca asked him never to speak of it.
Mr Kyrle read the confession and said they needed more witnesses.
Mrs Michelson and Hester Pinhorn signed statements about what they saw.
Marian copied her diary, and the Count's note, as evidence.
Mr Kyrle said Laura should go to Limmeridge to be known by all.
The three travelled north by train, with all their papers.
At Limmeridge, the villagers knew Laura and cried with joy.
The tenants cheered as Marian led Laura up to the house.
Mr Fairlie did not want to believe, but Walter showed the proofs.
Mr Fairlie gave way and signed a paper that named Laura his niece.
The false name on the tomb was changed to Anne Catherick.
Walter and Laura were married in the village church.
Walter and Laura had a baby son, and Marian loved him dearly.
When Mr Fairlie died, Laura's little son became the heir.
Years later, Walter walked the road where he first met Anne.
Walter wrote this story so that everyone would know the truth.
B1B2: Walter Hartright, a young drawing master, had spent the evening with his mother and sister in Hampstead. At midnight he set out for his rooms in London, walking alone down a quiet moonlit road.
Without any warning, a hand touched Walter's shoulder from behind. He spun around and saw a woman standing in the road, dressed in white from head to foot.
In a low and trembling voice, the stranger asked him whether she was on the road to London. He told her that she was, and offered to walk with her, but she begged him never to ask her any questions.
They walked on side by side along the empty road. Every time a leaf moved or a branch cracked, the woman glanced over her shoulder like a hunted animal.
The woman asked him whether he knew any gentlemen of title in London. When she named Sir Percival Glyde and Walter said that he had never heard of him, she seemed greatly relieved.
She told him that she had once been very happy in Cumberland, at a place called Limmeridge. There a kind lady named Mrs Fairlie had loved her, and had always dressed her in white.
At the edge of the city they passed the first lamps and the first houses. Walter stopped a passing cab, and the woman climbed in, thanking him again and again with tears in her eyes.
A few minutes later a carriage drew up beside the road, and a man leaned out to speak to a policeman. He asked whether anyone had seen a woman dressed in white pass by.
When Walter admitted that he had seen her, the men told him that she had escaped from an asylum. He had helped her to get away, and he did not know whether he had done right or wrong.
Walter reached his rooms very late, but he could not sleep. He kept seeing the pale face in the moonlight, and he could not decide whether she had been a sick woman or a wronged one.
A few days later, Walter's friend Pesca came running into his room, red-faced and out of breath. Pesca was a small, cheerful Italian who taught languages in London, and he never brought small news.

Pesca explained that one of his pupils knew a Mr Fairlie of Limmeridge House, who needed a drawing master for four months. When Walter heard the name Limmeridge he started, for it was the place the woman in white had spoken of.
That evening Walter told his mother and his sister Sarah about the offer, and about the woman he had met on the road. His mother looked uneasy and said that the meeting seemed to her like a bad sign.

Pesca came to the station to see Walter off, and he wept a little with joy. He had left Italy years ago for reasons he never explained, but he said that England had given him a friend, which was enough.
Walter travelled north all day, first by train and then by a slow coach. The towns were left behind and the hills grew higher, and he thought again about the pale face on the road.
Walter arrived at Limmeridge House as the sun was going down. It was a large, solid house of grey stone with a long front, and lamps were already shining in many of its windows.

A lady was standing by the window with her back to him, and her figure was as graceful as any he had ever seen. When she turned, he found a dark, strong face, but her eyes were so bright and kind that he forgot its plainness.

Over a late supper, Miss Halcombe explained the household to him. Her half-sister Laura was resting with a headache, and her uncle, Mr Fairlie, suffered so much from his nerves that he saw almost nobody.

Marian told him that he would mount and mend her uncle's drawings in the mornings, and teach the sisters to paint in the afternoons. She added without any shyness that she herself was the plain one, and that Laura was the beauty of the house.
In his room that night, Walter stood at the window and looked out over the moonlit hills. The silence was complete, and again he thought of the white figure on the road.
Mr Fairlie's valet, Louis, led Walter into a dim room full of rare coins and prints. There, wrapped in a shawl, sat a pale, thin man who winced at the sound of Walter's footsteps.

Mr Fairlie told Walter in a weary voice that he must mend and mount the drawings and teach his nieces. He added that Walter must speak softly, and that, whatever happened, he was never to be troubled about it.
Walter was given a bright room with tall windows, where hundreds of drawings lay piled on the tables. He began to sort and mend them, and he found that he enjoyed the quiet, patient work.
In the drawing room Walter first saw Laura Fairlie, who was sitting at the piano in a ray of sunlight. She was slender and fair, with soft blue eyes, and she rose with a shy smile to greet him.

The drawing lessons began on a bright afternoon, with paints and paper spread over a table. Marian learned quickly and made jokes about her mistakes, while Laura bent over her work with careful, gentle patience.
As the fine weather continued, the lessons moved outdoors to the garden and the moor. Laura spoke to Walter about her childhood, and about her father, whom she had loved very much.
In the evenings the three of them sat in the drawing room while Laura played the piano. Walter listened with his eyes half closed, and Marian watched him from her chair.
One night Walter had to admit to himself that he loved Laura. He knew that it was hopeless, because he was a poor drawing master, and she was the niece of a rich man.
One evening Walter told the sisters about the woman he had met on the road to London. Laura listened with wide eyes, but Marian turned pale when he said that the stranger had spoken of Mrs Fairlie.
At last Marian spoke, and her voice was low. She said that Mrs Fairlie had once taken a girl called Anne Catherick into the village school, and had loved to dress her in white.

Marian spent that night reading her mother's old letters, and in the morning she told Walter what she had found. Anne Catherick had been a slow, sweet child, and Mrs Fairlie had been kind to her for the sake of the girl's mother.
Walter and Marian agreed that the woman on the road must be Anne Catherick. Marian had learned from the letters that the child had been strangely like Laura, and the thought chilled them both.
A few days later a letter came for Laura in a handwriting that nobody knew. It told of a bad dream and warned her, in broken words, never to marry Sir Percival Glyde.
Marian told Walter, kindly but plainly, that Laura was to marry Sir Percival Glyde. Her father had wished it, and she had promised him on his deathbed that she would keep his wish.

Marian and Walter were sure that the letter had been written by Anne Catherick, who must be somewhere near. Walter went out to search the lanes, and a boy told him that he had seen a woman in white by the church.

At dusk Walter went to the churchyard and found the woman in white kneeling beside a white marble tomb. When she looked up, he saw to his astonishment that her face was like Laura's, but thin and sick.

Anne admitted that she had written the letter to Laura, because she wanted to save her from marriage. She said that Sir Percival had shut her up in an asylum because she knew a secret that could ruin him.
Anne saw Marian coming across the grass and ran away in terror before Walter could stop her. He followed her track to a farm called Todd's Corner, where a kind woman, Mrs Clements, opened the door.

When Walter returned to the house, Marian spoke to him very frankly. She said that Laura was promised to another man, and that for the sake of her honour he must leave Limmeridge, and he sadly agreed.
On his last evening Laura gave Walter a small drawing and said quietly that she must keep her promise. The next morning he left Limmeridge, and soon afterward he sailed for Central America.
Some months later the family lawyer, Mr Gilmore, came to Limmeridge to draw up Laura's marriage papers. He was an old and careful man who had known Laura since she was a child.
Mr Gilmore was struck by how pale and quiet Laura had become. When he asked whether she was happy about the marriage, she said that she would keep the promise she had made to her father.

Mr Gilmore asked Mr Fairlie for help, but Mr Fairlie said that he could not bear to be troubled. In the end Mr Gilmore gave way, and so if Laura died young, her fortune would pass to Sir Percival.
Mr Gilmore left Limmeridge feeling that he had failed in his duty. Marian promised herself that she would never let Laura out of her sight, whatever happened.
The wedding took place in the village church in the cold of December. Laura wore white, and her face was as pale as her dress, while Marian stood close beside her.

Laura wrote from Italy only rarely, and her short letters said nothing about being happy. Marian read them again and again, and she grew more worried with each month.
