The Count was very fond of his white mice. He let them run over his hands and up his sleeves, and he talked to them softly as if they were his children.
The Count also kept a cockatoo and two canaries, and he spent hours teaching them to sing. He loved sweet cakes, he made his own tea, and he sang opera airs in a surprisingly sweet voice.
Marian found that the Count could talk about books, politics and science with equal ease. She admitted in her diary that he was the most interesting man she had ever met, and she tried to resist him.
When Sir Percival lost his temper at dinner, the Count calmed him with a few quiet words. Marian saw that Sir Percival obeyed his guest like a boy, and that Madame Fosco watched everything.
Strange men began to call at the house and ask for Sir Percival, who always sent them away. Marian soon understood that he owed a great deal of money to a great many people.

One afternoon Sir Percival told Laura that she must sign a paper, which would help him to raise some money. When she asked what the paper said, he told her it was not a matter for a woman to understand.
The next morning, in the library, Sir Percival held out a paper folded to show only a line for a name. The Count and his wife stood nearby, ready to sign as witnesses.
Laura refused to sign anything without reading it first. Sir Percival struck the table with his hand and shouted that she had no right to question him, but she did not move.
The Count raised his hand and said gently that the signing could wait until everyone was calm. Sir Percival muttered something angry and stormed out of the room, slamming the door behind him.

That evening Marian wrote to Mr Fairlie and begged him to invite Laura home for a visit. His reply came quickly and said that he could not interfere between a husband and wife, because it would upset his nerves.

The next morning Sir Percival was cheerful and almost kind, and he said that he was sorry for his temper. Marian was not deceived, and she noticed that he and the Count whispered together whenever they could.
A farm boy slipped a folded note into Laura's hand in the garden. It was from Anne Catherick, who said that she was close by and begged to meet Laura at the old boathouse.
Marian thought that Laura should be careful, but she said that she must hear what Anne had to say. She walked down to the lake alone, while Marian waited among the fir trees nearby.
Inside the dim boathouse Anne waited in her white dress. When the two women stood face to face, the likeness was so strong that Laura felt she was looking in a mirror.
Anne told Laura that Sir Percival had a secret that could ruin him. She said that her mother knew it too, and that he had shut her up in the asylum to keep it hidden.
Anne offered to tell Laura the whole secret, if Laura would promise to tell nobody. Laura refused to keep any secret from Marian, and Anne hesitated and looked afraid.
Suddenly a shadow fell across the wall of the boathouse. Anne sprang up with a cry and ran away into the woods, saying that somebody had been watching them.
That evening Sir Percival, who had been told of the meeting by Madame Fosco, seized Laura by the arm. He demanded to know what Anne Catherick had said to her.
Marian pulled Sir Percival's hand from Laura's arm and stood between them. At that moment the Count entered the hall and, with a few smooth words, calmed Sir Percival once again.
Sir Percival sent men to search the woods and fields, but Anne had vanished without a trace. Marian decided that she must find out what Sir Percival and the Count were planning.
One hot, heavy night Marian heard voices below her window. The two men were talking on the terrace, so she climbed out onto the low roof of the veranda and lay down to listen.
Lying on the roof, Marian heard Sir Percival tell the Count that he needed money very soon. His creditors would not wait, and he was afraid that he would lose everything.

The Count answered calmly that Lady Glyde's money might still be obtained by other means. Sir Percival said in a low voice that there must be no violence, and the Count replied that of course there would be none.
The men spoke next about Anne Catherick, and about how much she looked like Lady Glyde. Then the wind rose and carried their words away, so that Marian could hear no more.
Suddenly the storm broke, and the rain came down in sheets. Marian could not move until the men left the terrace, and she lay on the roof, soaked to the skin.
When the men had gone, Marian crept back through her window, cold and shaking. She tore off her wet clothes, but she could not get warm, and she felt her head begin to burn.
By the light of a single candle Marian wrote in her diary all that she had heard. Her hand shook so badly that she could hardly hold the pen, and the words ran together before her eyes.
In the morning Laura found Marian lying in bed, hot with fever and half unconscious. A servant was sent at once to fetch the doctor, Mr Dawson.
Mr Dawson said that the fever was serious and would last for some time. The Count and Madame Fosco kindly offered to help with the nursing, and Laura gratefully accepted.
For many nights Laura sat beside Marian's bed while the fever raged. The whole house grew quiet, and Marian lay half asleep and said strange things that nobody could understand.
One night, while Marian lay ill, the Count crept into her room without a sound. He found her diary under her pillow, and he smiled as he took it out.
The Count read every page of the diary, nodding and smiling to himself. He learned all that Marian knew, and all that she feared, and he admired her cleverness.
Before he left, the Count wrote a long note at the end of the diary in his own bold hand. He praised Marian's cleverness and her courage, and he slipped the diary back under her pillow.
Sir Percival suddenly dismissed most of the servants, saying that he wished to save money. Mrs Michelson was sent to the seaside, and soon the great house was almost empty.
Laura begged to be allowed to sit with Marian, but the Count said that she must rest. She wrote to Mr Fairlie for help, but she later found that her letter had never been sent.
At last Marian woke, thin and pale and very weak. When she reached for her diary, she found the Count's note, and she understood that he had read every word.
Mr Dawson said that Marian was out of danger. The Count suggested kindly that she should go north to Limmeridge to recover in the clean air, and Mr Dawson agreed.
Marian was helped into a carriage with a nurse, still too weak to argue. As it drove away, she saw Laura waving from an upstairs window, and she felt a terrible fear for her sister.
After Marian had gone, the Count told Laura that Marian had been too weak to travel farther. She was resting at his house in London and wanted Laura to come to her at once.
The next day Laura left Blackwater Park alone and took the train to London. She watched the green fields run past the window and hoped that she would soon see her sister's face.
Meanwhile, in London, Anne Catherick had grown very ill, for her heart had always been weak. She had come to the city with her old friend Mrs Clements, and the journey had been too much for her.
The Count's wife found Anne in London, and she took her to the Count's house in St John's Wood. Anne was too weak and confused to refuse, and she was put to bed in an upstairs room.
Anne died during the night of her weak heart, on the twenty-fifth of July. The doctor, who had been told that she was Lady Glyde, wrote that name on the paper.
The next day Laura's train arrived in London, and the Count was waiting for her on the platform. He bowed with a smile and said that he would take her to her sister in his own carriage.
The cab drove through the busy streets to the Count's house in St John's Wood. Marian was not there, and Madame Fosco said that she had gone out for a little air and would soon return.
Madame Fosco gave Laura a cup of hot tea. It tasted rather strange, and soon Laura felt faint and dizzy, and the room began to turn around her until she fell.
Laura woke in a bare room, wearing plain clothes that were marked with Anne Catherick's name. A woman told her that she was Anne Catherick, an escaped patient, and that she must return to the asylum.
A closed carriage waited at the door, and Laura was led to it between two women. She said again and again that she was Lady Glyde, but they only shook their heads and told her to be calm.
At the gate of the asylum a doctor received Laura as Anne Catherick. When she said that she was really Lady Glyde, he smiled kindly and wrote the words in his book as a sign of her illness.
Day after day Laura lived among strangers in the asylum. The nurses were kind and firm, but every time she told the truth, they said it was part of her illness.
A few days later a letter with a black edge came to Limmeridge. It said that Lady Glyde had died suddenly in London of a disease of the heart.
Marian was overcome with grief and horror at the news. Mr Fairlie wept loudly, but he complained even more about what the news had done to his nerves.
Sir Percival wrote that Lady Glyde was to be buried beside her mother at Limmeridge. A hearse brought the coffin north, and the villagers stood in silence as it passed.
The funeral took place on a grey morning, and the villagers wept as the coffin was lowered into the vault. The marble above it was to be marked with the name of Laura, Lady Glyde.
After the funeral Marian stayed alone at the tomb and looked at the new name. She could not feel that Laura was truly beneath it, and a small voice in her mind said that something was wrong.
That night Marian read her diary again, and the Count's note in it. She began to see how carefully the Count had planned every step, and how she had been sent out of the way.
A few days later Mrs Clements arrived at Limmeridge in great distress. She said that Anne Catherick had vanished from London, and that she had searched everywhere without finding her.
Marian listened closely to Mrs Clements, and her excitement grew with every word. Anne had vanished just as Laura was said to have died, and perhaps the woman in the tomb was Anne.
Marian did not tell Mr Fairlie her suspicions, because she knew that he would not believe her. She travelled to London alone, but she found the Count's house empty, with the Count and his wife gone.
Mrs Clements knew where Anne had been kept before. Marian went to the same asylum and asked whether a new patient had been brought there, in a carriage, in the last few days.
The porter refused to answer Marian's questions, and the doctor of the asylum would not see her. He said that no visitors were allowed, and that he could say nothing about his patients.
Marian waited near the gate until a nurse came out, and she offered the woman money. The nurse said that a new patient had arrived a few days ago, and that the woman kept saying she was Lady Glyde.
The nurse told Marian that the patients walked in the garden every evening. For a larger sum she let Marian into a corner where she could watch without being seen.
Marian stepped out of the shadow and saw that the thin woman was Laura. Laura looked at her with dazed eyes, and then she whispered her sister's name and fell into her arms.
Marian could not bear to leave Laura there for one more night. She paid the nurse to open the garden door that night, and she promised that a cab would be waiting outside.
At midnight Marian stood in the lane beside a waiting cab, and listened. The night was cold and silent, and every minute felt as long as an hour.
At last a small door opened in the wall, and the nurse pushed Laura out into the lane. Marian caught her in her arms, and the door closed behind her without a word.
Marian and Mrs Clements helped Laura into the cab and told the driver to go quickly. The horse trotted away through the empty streets, and nobody came after them.
Laura slept for almost a whole day in Marian's lodgings. When she woke, she told Marian about the tea, the strange room, the false name and the asylum, and Marian listened in horror.
Marian had very little money, and Laura's memory was still weak and confused. She promised herself that nobody would ever take her sister away again, and she thought of Walter Hartright, far away.
Walter came home from Central America after many months of danger and sickness. He was thin and brown, and he had learned a great deal about courage, but he had not forgotten Laura.
Walter hurried to Hampstead, where his mother and sister welcomed him with tears of joy. But when he asked about Limmeridge, they looked at each other, and his sister said that Lady Glyde was dead.
Walter travelled north to Limmeridge and went at once to the churchyard. There he found the white tomb with its new inscription, and he read Laura's name with tears in his eyes.
As Walter sat by the tomb, two women in thick veils entered the churchyard. He did not wish to be seen in his grief, so he stepped behind a tree and waited for them to pass.
At the tomb one of the women lifted her veil, and Walter saw Laura's face. He thought at first that it was a ghost, and then he saw that she was alive.
Walter stepped out from behind the tree, and Marian cried out when she saw him. Laura looked at him slowly, as if she were trying to remember where she had seen his face.
Marian told Walter the whole terrible story in low words among the gravestones. He learned that it was Anne Catherick, and not Laura, who lay in the tomb under Laura's name.
Walter brought Marian and Laura back to London and found them cheap rooms in a quiet street near his own. The rooms were small and poor, but there they were safe from Sir Percival.
The three lived quietly on very little money in those days. Marian did needlework, Laura began to draw again, slowly, and Walter worked long hours, selling his drawings to anyone who would buy them.
One evening Walter stood before the sisters and made a solemn promise. He swore that he would prove who Laura was, and that Sir Percival and the Count would answer for what they had done.
Walter went to a London lawyer named Mr Kyrle and told him the whole story. The lawyer listened carefully, with his fingers pressed together, and asked a great many questions.

Mr Kyrle said that he believed Walter, but that the law would need strong proof. The certificate, the funeral and the tomb all said that Lady Glyde was dead, and a woman who said otherwise might be thought mad.
Mr Kyrle said that the date on the certificate was the weak point in the plot. If they could prove that Laura was alive after that day, the certificate would be shown to be false.
That evening Walter asked Laura gently about the day she left Blackwater Park. She remembered the train and the Count's smile, but the day and the date were lost in her mind.
Walter visited Mrs Clements and asked about Anne's last days. She told him how Anne had grown ill in London, and how she had come back from an errand to find her gone.

Mrs Clements told Walter that Anne had often spoken of her mother and of the village of Welmingham in Hampshire. Anne had always believed that Sir Percival's secret had something to do with the church there.
Walter found Hester Pinhorn, who had been the Count's cook in St John's Wood. She remembered a sick lady who had died in the house on the twenty-fifth of July.

Walter counted the days and saw that Anne had died on the twenty-fifth, but Laura had only reached London on the twenty-sixth. The certificate was false, but Mr Kyrle said that more proof was still needed.
Walter and Marian agreed that they must find Sir Percival's secret. If they could discover what Anne had known, they might force him to confess what he had done.
Early the next morning Walter said goodbye to Laura and Marian. Laura pressed a small gift into his hand, and he took the train south to Hampshire.
Walter reached the village of Welmingham in Hampshire at the end of a long, hot day. It was a quiet place of low houses and green fields, with an old grey church at one end of the street.
At the church door Walter met the old parish clerk, a wrinkled and nearly deaf man who loved to talk. The clerk was delighted to have a visitor, and he agreed to show Walter around the church.
The clerk unlocked the door of a small room beside the church, called the vestry. Inside stood an iron press, and in it were the old books in which every marriage was written down.
Walter asked the clerk for the register that recorded the marriage of Sir Felix Glyde, the father of Sir Percival. He turned the heavy pages until he found the entry.
Looking closely, Walter saw that the ink of the entry was different from the entries around it. The lines were crowded between two others, as though they had been squeezed in later.
Walter copied the entry word for word onto a sheet of paper, while the old clerk dozed in his chair. He felt more and more sure that someone had forged it.
When the clerk woke up he spoke of Mr Catherick, who had been clerk before him and had kept the vestry key. Mrs Catherick had left the village in disgrace, and now she lived in Southampton.
Walter took the train to Southampton and asked his way to Mrs Catherick's house. He found a neat little house with spotless windows in a quiet street, and he knocked at the door.
Mrs Catherick was a proud, stern woman who received Walter coldly in her tidy parlour. She said that Sir Percival Glyde had always been generous to her, and she would not hear a word against him.
When Walter spoke of Anne, Mrs Catherick lost her temper. In her anger she let slip that Sir Percival had no right to the name he used, and then she was silent.
After Walter left, Mrs Catherick sat down and wrote a hurried letter to Sir Percival. She warned him that a young man had visited her and was asking questions about his name.
Back in London Walter told Marian about the register and Mrs Catherick. That evening Pesca came to see him and invited him to the opera, and Walter accepted gladly, for he badly needed a rest.
In the middle of the opera Pesca suddenly turned pale and stared at a large man sitting in a box across the theatre. His whole body began to tremble, and he held Walter's arm tightly.

In the corridor Pesca whispered that the fat man was a traitor to a secret society called the Brotherhood. He said that he himself was a member, and that if the traitor saw him, they were both in danger.
Just then the fat man looked across the theatre and saw Pesca. He rose slowly from his seat and left the box, and Walter, remembering Marian's words, knew that this was Count Fosco.
Walter feared that Sir Percival, once warned, would try to destroy the register. He went back to Welmingham and waited near the old church to see what would happen.
Late that night Sir Percival hurried to the church and let himself into the vestry with a false key. He carried a lantern, and he went straight to the iron press where the registers were kept.
Inside the vestry Sir Percival tore out the page of the register. As he worked, his lantern set fire to the dry papers, and in a moment the little room was full of flames and smoke.
The villagers ran toward the burning church with buckets of water, and Walter threw himself at the door. He and the old clerk tried again and again to break it down, but the fire was too strong.

When the fire was out, Sir Percival Glyde was found dead in the vestry. The coroner decided that it had been an accident, and Walter, who had wished him to answer for his crimes, felt no triumph at all.
Walter found out where Count Fosco was lodging, in a quiet street in London. He climbed the stairs to the Count's rooms with his heart beating fast and a plan in his mind.
The Count received Walter with perfect politeness, in the middle of his birds and his white mice. Walter told him plainly that he knew about the plot against Laura, and about the false certificate.
Walter said that his friend Pesca had recognised the Count as a traitor to the Brotherhood. For the first time the Count's calm face lost its colour, and his smile disappeared.
Walter offered the Count a bargain on the spot. If the Count wrote a full confession of the plot, he would be given a few hours to leave England before anyone was told.
The Count sat at a large table and wrote all night, with a white mouse on his shoulder. Now and then he stopped to drink coffee and to joke gently about his own cleverness.
Madame Fosco sat quietly in a corner during the whole night. She never took her eyes from her husband, and Walter felt a strange pity for her.
The Count's account told the whole story of the plot. It described how Anne died in his house, how Laura was lured to London, and how she was sent to the asylum as Anne.
The confession gave all the dates in careful order. It showed that Laura was still alive on the twenty-sixth of July, though the certificate had said that she died on the twenty-fifth.
At dawn the Count finished and signed his name with a great flourish. He handed over the pages with a polite bow, and said that he admired Walter's courage.
Walter took the pages home through the early morning streets. He had promised to keep silent for a few hours, and he kept his word, even though he hated the Count.
Marian and Laura read the Count's confession together at the little table. Marian was angry at its proud tone, but she was also full of hope, for here at last was real proof.
The Count and his wife left England the same day on a steamer for France. Walter kept his promise and said nothing for several hours, though he longed to tell Pesca at once.
Some weeks later Walter read a short paragraph in a newspaper. It told of an unknown man, very large, who had been found dead in a Paris street, and who had not been identified.
At the Paris morgue Walter saw the great body of Count Fosco lying quietly among the dead. There was a mark on his arm, and Walter knew that the Brotherhood had killed him as a traitor.
Back in London, Walter told Pesca what he had seen. Pesca sat quietly with his hands over his face, and then asked Walter never to speak of the Brotherhood again.
Mr Kyrle read the confession twice, and then he said that it was a very strong piece of evidence. He advised Walter to gather more witnesses, so that nobody could doubt the truth.
Walter found Mrs Michelson, the housekeeper from Blackwater Park, and Hester Pinhorn, the Count's cook. Both agreed to sign statements telling what they had seen and the dates when it happened.
Marian copied out her diary, with the Count's note in it, so that it could be kept as evidence. It showed what had been planned at Blackwater Park, in the Count's own hand.
Mr Kyrle said that the best proof of all would be Laura's face. If the people of Limmeridge, who had known her since childhood, recognised her, then her uncle could no longer deny it.

The three travelled north by train to Limmeridge, carrying the box of papers with them. Laura was clearer in her mind than she had been for many months, and she looked out of the window with quiet interest.
At Limmeridge the villagers and tenants gathered around Laura in the lane. They knew her at once, and many of them wept with joy to see her alive.
The tenants followed Laura all the way to Limmeridge House, cheering as they came. Marian led her up the steps and through the front door, which the servants held open with wondering faces.
In his room Mr Fairlie at first refused to believe that Laura was alive. Walter laid the papers in front of him, and the voices of the tenants outside showed him that he could not deny her.
At last Mr Fairlie gave way and signed a paper that declared Laura to be his niece. He complained that the whole business had been very bad for his nerves, but nobody listened to him.
The false name was cut away from the white tomb, and a mason carved a new inscription. At last poor Anne Catherick was remembered under her own name.
Walter and Laura were married in the same little church where Laura had once been married against her will. This time she was glad, and Marian stood by her side with tears of joy.
In time Walter and Laura had a baby boy. Marian loved him as dearly as if he were her own, and she spent hours watching over his cradle.
When Mr Fairlie died at last, his property passed to Laura's son. The little boy became the heir to Limmeridge, and the old house had a family again.
Years later Walter walked along the same road where he had first met Anne Catherick. He remembered her with kindness, and he thought of how much had come from that single midnight meeting.
Walter wrote down the whole story so that the world would know the truth about Laura. It began on a lonely road in the moonlight, and it ended in a happy home.

The road lay empty and silver beneath the moon, and the only sounds were his own footsteps and the faint stirring of the leaves. He swung round and found himself face to face with a woman who stood perfectly still in the moonlight, dressed from head to foot in white. When Walter assured her that it was, and offered to walk beside her through the dark, she accepted with a look of deep relief. She added, in a tone that was almost a plea, that he must promise never to ask her who she was or where she had come from.

They walked together along the silent road, and Walter noticed that the stranger's manner was gentle and her speech that of an educated person. Yet at every rustle in the hedge she glanced fearfully over her shoulder, like a hunted creature that dreads the sound of the dogs. He felt a strange mixture of pity and curiosity, and wondered what could have driven her out alone at such an hour.

After a long silence, the woman asked Walter whether he knew many people in London, and whether any of them were gentlemen of rank and title. Walter named a few, and then she asked, with a breathless eagerness, whether one of them was a baronet called Sir Percival Glyde. When he told her that he had never heard the name, her whole body seemed to loosen with relief, and he wondered what that name could mean to her.

The stranger's voice grew softer as she spoke of the only happy time she had ever known, a school at Limmeridge in the far north of England. There, she told him, a Mrs Fairlie had been so good to her that she had never forgotten it, and the kind lady had loved to see her dressed in white. Walter listened without understanding why her words made him uneasy, for the names meant nothing to him yet.

When the first lamps and the dark shapes of houses appeared, the woman begged to be left to go on alone, for she said that she would now be safe. Walter stopped a passing cab, helped her inside and paid the driver, and she thanked him over and over in a voice that was close to tears. As the cab rolled away, she leaned out for one moment, and her white face seemed to float in the darkness.

Hardly had the cab disappeared when a carriage clattered up behind Walter and drew to a halt beside the road. A man leaned from its window and put a sharp question to a passing policeman, asking whether he had seen a woman dressed all in white go by that way. Walter's heart sank, for he understood at once that the woman had been telling the truth about being followed.

They thanked him coldly and drove off in the direction the cab had taken, while Walter stood in the road with a troubled conscience. Had he done a kindness to a frightened woman, or a wrong to a sick one who was now at the mercy of her enemies?

Walter reached his rooms long after midnight, yet sleep refused to come, for the pale face and the trembling voice rose before him every time he closed his eyes. He turned the strange meeting over and over, weighing the woman's fear against the men's calm explanation, and he could not decide which of them to believe. Only one thing was certain: he would never forget that night on the moonlit road, and he had a feeling that he had not seen the last of her.

A few days later, Walter's friend Pesca came bursting into his room, red in the face and almost too excited to speak. Pesca explained that one of his pupils was a friend of a Mr Fairlie, who owned a large house called Limmeridge in the county of Cumberland. At the name Limmeridge Walter started, for it was the very place the pale stranger had named on the moonlit road, and he could hardly believe such a coincidence.

That evening Walter went out to Hampstead and told his mother and his sister Sarah about the splendid offer, and then, a little shyly, about the woman in white and the name she had spoken. Pesca insisted on carrying Walter's bag to the station, and on the platform he kissed his friend on both cheeks and wept without the least embarrassment. Years before, for reasons that he had never explained, he had left Italy, and Walter had learned never to ask him what he had left behind. Yet Pesca declared, with his hand over his heart, that England had given him one good friend, and that this was worth more than a kingdom.

All day the train carried Walter northward, through grey towns and green fields, and then a slow coach took him on into a wilder country of hills and open sky. The air grew sharper, the villages smaller and the hills higher, until London seemed to belong to another world. In spite of the beauty outside the window, his thoughts kept returning to the pale woman in white, and he could not shake off a feeling that she had somehow sent him here.

It was almost evening when Walter reached Limmeridge, and the long grey front of the house stood out solid and calm against a sky streaked with red. Lights were already glowing in many of the windows, and beyond the garden the dark line of the hills closed in the view. A servant took his bags at the door and led him, through a hall that smelled of old wood and beeswax, to a room where someone was waiting.

A lady stood by the window with her back to him, and Walter, seeing the curve of her waist and the grace of her movements, thought that he had never beheld a more perfect figure. Then she turned, and he saw a dark, strong, almost masculine face, with a square jaw and a faint shadow on the lip, but her brown eyes were so frank and clever that the plainness was forgotten at once. She held out her hand like a man and said, with a smile, that she was Marian Halcombe, and that she hoped they would be friends.

Over a late supper Marian explained the little world of Limmeridge with the same plain honesty that marked all her talk. Her half-sister Laura was resting with a headache, and the master of the house, her uncle Mr Fairlie, was so troubled by his nerves that a closing door could make him ill. She added, with a laugh, that Walter would soon learn to walk on tiptoe and to speak in whispers, as every servant in the house had done.

Marian told him that he would spend his mornings mounting and repairing her uncle's great collection of drawings, and his afternoons teaching the two sisters to sketch and to paint. She spoke of her own looks without any shyness, saying that nature had given her the brains and her half-sister the beauty, and that he might as well know it from the start. Walter, who had rarely heard a woman speak so openly, liked her immediately for it.

That night, in the quiet bedroom they had given him, Walter stood at the window and gazed out across the garden to the hills silvered by the moon. The silence of the house was so deep that he could hear his own breathing, and the same pale light that had shone on the road near London now lay over this far northern valley. He wondered what link could possibly join the stranger in white to this peaceful household, and then, tired from his long journey, he went to bed and slept.

Mr Fairlie's valet, a soft-footed man named Louis, led Walter into a half-darkened room filled with glass cases of rare coins and portfolios of valuable prints. In the middle of it all sat the master of Limmeridge, a pale, thin gentleman wrapped in a shawl, who winced at the sound of Walter's boots as though they were thunder. He sighed that he was a martyr to his nerves, and held up a delicate hand as if to keep the whole world at a distance.

In a weary, drawling voice, Mr Fairlie explained that Walter was to mend and mount his drawings, to instruct the young ladies, and to avoid all noise, haste and difficulty. He declared that he disliked being asked for decisions, and that every question should go to Miss Halcombe, who was far more robust than he could ever hope to be. Then he closed his eyes to show that the conversation was over, and Walter was glad to escape into the corridor.

The room set aside for his work was bright and airy, with tall windows facing the garden, and on its long tables lay hundreds of drawings in every state of neglect. Walter soon fell into a quiet rhythm of sorting, cleaning and mending, and he discovered that the careful labour calmed his mind. By the end of the first week the heaps were beginning to take shape, and he was already looking forward to the afternoons, when his real teaching would begin.

In the sunny drawing room Walter first saw Laura Fairlie, sitting at the piano with the light falling on her hair and her slender hands moving softly over the keys. She was fair and delicate, with eyes of a clear and gentle blue, and when she rose to greet him she coloured a little, as though she were not used to meeting strangers. Marian, standing beside her like a shadow beside a flower, said that this was her half-sister, and Walter bowed with a feeling that he had never known before.

The first lesson took place on a bright afternoon, with paper, brushes and paint boxes spread over a large table in the morning room. Marian learned with a bold and impatient cleverness, laughing at her own mistakes, while her half-sister worked slowly and delicately, her fair head bent low over her paper. Walter found that the sisters were as different as two people could be, and that both were a delight to teach.

In the long fine days of summer the lessons moved out of doors, to the garden and the open moor beyond it, where Marian often sat reading in the sun while her sister sketched. Laura talked to Walter in her soft voice about her quiet childhood, about the mother she hardly remembered and the father she had adored, and he listened more than he drew. Without either of them noticing, the weeks passed, and the talk of teacher and pupil grew into something warmer.

When the lamps were lit, the three of them gathered in the drawing room, and Laura played the piano while the long northern twilight faded from the windows. Walter sat very still, with his eyes half closed, and let the music wash over him, aware of nothing in the room but the sound of her playing. Marian, with her book open and unread upon her knee, watched the two of them with a thoughtful and anxious expression.

One night, sitting alone in his room, Walter was forced to admit what his heart had known for weeks, that he loved Laura Fairlie with his whole soul. It was a hopeless love, for he was only a poor drawing master with his living to earn, while she was a rich man's niece who would one day marry far above him. He resolved to hide his feelings and to do his duty, and he threw himself into his work with a fierce and almost desperate energy.

One evening, when the talk turned to strange happenings, Walter told the sisters the whole story of the woman in white and the midnight road. Laura listened with wide, frightened eyes, but Marian grew pale and sat bolt upright when he mentioned that the stranger had spoken of Limmeridge and of a Mrs Fairlie who had been kind to her. When he came to the end of his tale, the room was silent, and for a long moment nobody in it said a single word.

At last Marian spoke, and her voice was lower than Walter had ever heard it. She said that Mrs Fairlie, the mother of both sisters, had once taken a poor child named Anne Catherick into the village school, and had been so fond of the girl that she dressed her always in white. She rose abruptly, saying that she must look through her mother's old letters that very night, and the others watched her go with a strange feeling of dread.

Marian sat up half the night over a box of her mother's old letters, and in the morning she told Walter what she had learned. Anne Catherick had been a backward but affectionate child, and Mrs Fairlie had befriended her out of kindness to the girl's mother, a woman who lived in Hampshire. She added, with a frown, that she could not understand why a letter written so many years ago should make her feel afraid.

Walter and Marian agreed that the woman on the moonlit road could only have been Anne Catherick, grown to womanhood. The old letters also mentioned, almost in passing, that the little girl had borne a remarkable likeness to Laura as a child, and as Walter remembered the pale face in the moonlight, the thought sent a chill through him. Neither of them could say what such a likeness might mean, but both felt that it meant something.

A few days later, at breakfast, a letter arrived for Laura in a handwriting that no one at Limmeridge knew, and she turned white as she read it. The writer described a dream in which Laura stood at the altar in a church beside a man who meant her harm, and she begged the young lady, in broken and urgent words, never to marry Sir Percival Glyde. Marian took the letter from her trembling hand and read it through twice with a darkening face.

Marian drew Walter aside and told him, as gently as she could, that Laura was engaged to be married to Sir Percival Glyde, the very man named in the letter. The match had been arranged long ago by Laura's father, and on his deathbed she had given her word that she would not refuse it. Walter, who had hoped against hope that his feelings were secret, felt the ground fall away beneath him, and could not trust himself to answer.

Marian felt certain that Anne Catherick had written the letter, and that its author must be hiding somewhere in the neighbourhood. She asked Walter, who had seen the woman and would know her again, to search the lanes and fields around Limmeridge before anyone else found her. After a long day's walking, a boy told him that he had seen a pale woman dressed in white sitting by the churchyard wall.

At dusk Walter went to the quiet churchyard, and there, beside a white marble tomb, he found the woman in white wiping the stone with a cloth. He spoke to her gently, and when she turned her face to the last light, he saw with a shock that her features were Laura's own, though thinner, sadder and marked by some long illness. It was the tomb of Mrs Fairlie, and the stranger declared that she had come to keep it clean because Mrs Fairlie had been her only friend.

Anne admitted, with a shy and trembling candour, that she had written the letter to Laura, because she could not bear the thought of Mrs Fairlie's daughter becoming Sir Percival's wife. She told Walter that this man had shut her up in an asylum because she knew a secret about him, a secret so terrible that it could destroy his good name if it were told. When Walter pressed her to say what it was, she shook her head and said only that she had given her word, and that she was afraid.

As the dusk deepened, Anne caught sight of a figure approaching across the grass, and, without a word, she fled into the dark fields like a frightened deer. Walter followed her track as best he could, and it brought him at last to a lonely farm called Todd's Corner, where a kindly woman named Mrs Clements opened the door. She was Anne's old friend, she said, and she had taken the poor girl in when she came north, hoping to save her from those who wished to shut her up again.

When Walter returned to the house, Marian spoke to him with frankness and kindness, for she had seen what he tried so hard to conceal. She said that Laura belonged to another man by her own word, and that, for the sake of both of them, he must leave Limmeridge as soon as it could decently be arranged. Walter, who knew in his heart that she was right, bowed his head and agreed.

On his last evening in the garden, Laura gave Walter a small drawing she had made herself and told him, in a voice that shook, that she must keep her promise to her father. Early the next morning he took leave of Marian, who pressed his hand warmly, and he drove away from Limmeridge without once daring to look back. A few weeks later, hoping that distance would heal him, he sailed from England as a draughtsman on an expedition to the ruined cities of Central America.

Some months after Walter's departure, the family lawyer, Mr Gilmore, arrived at Limmeridge to prepare the papers for Laura's marriage. He was an elderly, careful gentleman who had known the Fairlies for many years, and he had a particular affection for the young heiress, whom he had known since she was a child. He had come to see that her fortune was properly protected, and he intended to do his duty with the greatest care.

Mr Gilmore was struck by the change in Laura, who seemed paler, quieter and older than the girl he remembered. When he asked her, as gently as an old lawyer could, whether she was truly content with the marriage, she answered in a steady voice that she meant to keep the promise she had made to her father. He did not find the answer comforting, but he could see that she would say nothing more.

Marian handed Mr Gilmore the anonymous letter that had warned Laura against her future husband, and she told him the little she knew about Anne Catherick. The old lawyer read it with a grave face and decided that Sir Percival, in fairness, should be given the chance to answer such a charge before the wedding took place. He therefore wrote to Sir Percival's lawyer, a Mr Merriman, and he waited anxiously for the reply.

Sir Percival's answer came promptly, and it was so calm and reasonable that Mr Gilmore felt his doubts melting away. He explained that Anne Catherick was a poor, weak-minded woman, that he had placed her in an asylum only at the request of her mother, Mrs Catherick, and he enclosed the mother's letter as proof. Marian, reading the page over the lawyer's shoulder, noted that it explained everything and yet convinced her of nothing.

Soon afterward Sir Percival himself arrived at Limmeridge, an alert, restless gentleman in middle life, with thinning hair, a ready smile and the easy manners of a man used to company. He was charming to Marian, respectful to Mr Gilmore and attentive to his bride, who received his courtesies with a polite and distant coldness that she made no effort to hide. Marian watched him closely, and decided that she could neither like nor dislike him as yet.

Mr Gilmore insisted that Laura's fortune should be tied up so that, if she died without children, it would return to her own family. Mr Merriman, on behalf of Sir Percival, argued just as firmly that a husband had a right to all of his wife's money, and the two lawyers went on disputing the point for several days. Mr Gilmore saw clearly that the question mattered a great deal, and that Sir Percival seemed to care about it more than he cared about his bride.

Mr Gilmore appealed to Laura's uncle to stand firm for his niece, but Mr Fairlie only fluttered a thin hand and complained that the whole affair was ruining his nerves. Without the head of the family behind him, the old lawyer had no power to refuse, and he was forced to accept the terms. By the final agreement, if Laura died, her fortune would pass to her husband, and Mr Gilmore signed with a heavy heart.

Mr Gilmore drove away from Limmeridge in low spirits, for he felt that he had been beaten by the weakness of one man and the cleverness of another. Before he left, he told Marian that he had done all he could, and that she must keep a watchful eye on her sister. Marian, who needed no such reminder, promised herself that she would stay close to Laura through everything that followed.

The wedding took place in the little village church at Limmeridge on a cold December morning, with the villagers crowding the benches to see their young lady married. Laura wore white, and her face was almost as pale as her dress, and she spoke her vows in a voice so low that the clergyman had to bend his head to hear it. Marian stood close beside her, and signed the register after them with a hand that did not shake, though her heart was heavy.

Soon after the ceremony the couple set out on a tour that would keep them in Italy for six months, and Marian stood on the steps and watched the carriage until it vanished around the bend. She had promised to join her sister at Sir Percival's country house when they returned, and meanwhile she must stay at Limmeridge with Mr Fairlie, who grew more fretful every day. In the long quiet months, she waited for Laura's letters like a woman waiting for news from a distant war.

Laura's letters from Italy arrived rarely and were always brief, full of descriptions of churches and views, and strangely empty of any word about her own happiness. Marian read each one over and over, searching between the lines for the real state of her sister's heart, and with every month her uneasiness deepened. She could not shake off the feeling that Laura was hiding something, and that Sir Percival's pleasant manners had a darker side.

In June the couple returned from Italy, and Marian travelled south to Sir Percival's house in Hampshire to join them, as she had promised. She hurried to embrace her sister, and was shocked to find that Laura had grown thin and quiet, and that her smile came slowly and seemed to cost her an effort. Sir Percival, standing by, remarked cheerfully that married life suited his wife, but the words did not sound true.

Blackwater Park was a large and gloomy old house, half hidden among tall trees whose branches seemed to press against the windows. Behind the garden a dark lake lay under a screen of fir woods, with an old boathouse at its edge, and one whole wing of the building had been shut up for years and was said to be haunted. Marian, who was not easily frightened, felt a chill as she walked through the echoing halls.

The housekeeper, Mrs Michelson, proved to be a stiff, respectable woman who saw everything and spoke of nothing, and Marian could not decide whether she was a friend or a spy. She also discovered that Sir Percival's pleasant manners disappeared the moment the guests went home, and that he shouted at the servants and slammed doors in a way he had never done at Limmeridge. Laura listened to every one of his outbursts with a lowered head, and she said nothing, as if she had long ago learned that silence was her only protection.

That night Marian sat on the edge of Laura's bed, and by the light of a single candle she asked her sister, quietly, whether she was happy. Laura admitted, after a long silence, that she was trying to be a good wife, but that her husband was often angry with her, and that there was a part of her heart that she could never give him. Marian kissed her forehead and promised that she would not leave her, whatever Sir Percival might say.

One morning Sir Percival read a letter at breakfast and announced, with an odd mixture of pleasure and uneasiness, that his friend Count Fosco was coming to stay with his wife. Madame Fosco was Laura's aunt, the sister of Mr Fairlie, and Marian remembered her as a talkative and rather foolish woman who had married an Italian nobleman abroad. Mrs Michelson was told to prepare the best rooms, and the household began to bustle with the work of welcome.

Madame Fosco arrived before her husband, stepping from the carriage in a plain dress and sitting down with a stiff and dignified air that was entirely new. The silly, chattering woman Marian remembered had vanished, and in her place sat a cold, silent figure who spoke only when spoken to and whose eyes followed her husband's every movement. Marian could not decide whether the change was a mark of respect or a sign of fear.

Count Fosco was the largest man Marian had ever seen, and yet he stepped from the carriage with the lightness of a dancer and spoke in a soft, almost motherly voice. He had a great head, a clever face and a pair of large, steady grey eyes, and he carried with him a cage of white mice, a cockatoo and two canaries, which he treated as if they were precious guests. Marian felt herself being studied, and took an immediate and reluctant interest in him.

In ten minutes the Count had charmed the entire household, kissing Laura's hand, bowing to Marian and speaking so kindly to Mrs Michelson that the old housekeeper actually smiled. He praised the house, the lake and the weather with an easy grace, and even Sir Percival, who had been ill-tempered all week, relaxed in his presence. Marian found herself liking him against her will, and at the same moment she felt a cold fear rise within her.

At the first dinner the Count told stories of his travels with such humour and warmth that even Laura laughed, while Sir Percival, strangely quiet, ate almost nothing and watched his guest like a servant watching his master. That night, in her own room, Marian opened her diary and wrote that she was beginning to fear the Count more than any man she had ever met. She could not have said why, except that his kindness seemed too perfect to be real.

The Count's chief delight was his family of white mice, which he trained to run over his hands, up his sleeves and across the great expanse of his waistcoat at the sound of his voice. He talked to them in a soft, fond murmur, and kissed their little pink noses with the tenderness of a father. Marian watched this performance with amazement, wondering how a man of such dainty affections could be so large and so powerful.

The Count also kept a cockatoo and two canaries, which he fed with sugar from his fingers and taught to sing in time with his own surprisingly sweet voice. He took an enormous pleasure in cakes, sweets and cream, prepared his tea himself with the care of a chemist, and settled each day into the largest chair in the house with the contentment of a cat. Whatever he did, he did with such grace and good humour that it was almost impossible for anyone to dislike him.

Marian soon discovered that the Count could talk with equal ease about books, science, politics and the follies of mankind, and he listened to her opinions with a courtesy that few men had ever shown her. In her diary she admitted, with some annoyance, that he was the most fascinating man she had ever met, and that she felt herself being drawn toward him in spite of herself. She resolved that she would be on her guard, and that she would never forget what she had seen in his eyes.

One evening Sir Percival flew into a rage over a spilled glass of wine, and with a few quiet words the Count reduced him to sullen silence, as one might quiet a child. Marian noted that her brother-in-law, who bullied his servants and frightened his wife, obeyed his guest like a boy obeying his tutor. Madame Fosco, sitting with her hands folded, observed the whole scene with a calm and attentive eye, and said not a word.

Strange men in plain black coats began to appear at the door and ask for Sir Percival, who always ordered the servants to send them away with an excuse. Marian gathered, from the housekeeper's hints and from Sir Percival's black moods, that he owed a great deal of money to a great many people, and that he was running out of time. This helped to explain why he had been in such haste to marry an heiress.

One afternoon Sir Percival informed Laura, with a forced smile, that she would be asked to sign a paper in the library the next morning, which would help him to raise some money. When she asked what the paper contained, he replied rather sharply that it was a business matter, and not one that a woman could be expected to understand. Laura said, in her soft voice, that she would like to read it before she signed, and a dangerous silence fell upon the room.

The next morning, in the library, Sir Percival held out a long paper that had been folded in such a way that only a blank space for a signature could be seen. The Count and Madame Fosco stood beside him as witnesses, the Count with his hands calmly folded over his waistcoat, and Marian, who had insisted on being present, watched them all with narrowed eyes. Laura looked at the folded sheet and at her husband, and her face grew very pale.

Laura said, quietly but firmly, that she would not sign any paper whose contents she was not allowed to read. Sir Percival struck the table so hard that the inkstand jumped, and he shouted that a wife had no right to question her husband, but Laura did not move, and Marian stepped forward to stand by her side. Even the Count was silent for a moment, as if he were measuring the young woman's courage.

At last the Count raised one large hand and said, in his softest voice, that it would be a pity to quarrel over a mere formality, and that the signing might wait until everyone was calm. Sir Percival glared at him, muttered something under his breath and stormed out of the room, slamming the door so hard that the glass rattled. Laura sank into a chair, trembling from head to foot, and Marian put an arm around her shoulders.

That evening Marian wrote to Mr Fairlie, begging him to invite Laura to Limmeridge for a long visit, and thus to take her out of her husband's reach. His reply, which arrived within days, said that he could not possibly interfere between husband and wife, since the very thought of trouble was ruining his nerves. Marian crumpled the letter in her fist, and understood that she and Laura now stood quite alone.

On the following morning Sir Percival was as cheerful as a sunny day, and he apologised handsomely to Laura for what he called a moment of bad temper. Marian was not deceived for an instant, for she noticed that he and the Count kept whispering together in corners, and fell silent whenever she approached. The peace that now lay over Blackwater Park seemed to her the stillness before a storm.

A farm boy slipped a crumpled note into Laura's hand as she walked in the garden, and Laura read it with a beating heart. It was from Anne Catherick, who wrote that she was living not far away, that she knew a secret that concerned Laura's safety, and that she begged her to come alone to the old boathouse by the lake. Laura took the note to Marian at once, and the two sisters whispered over it.

Marian was afraid that the note might be a trap, but Laura was moved by the thought of the frightened woman in white and said that she must hear what Anne had to say. She walked down toward the lake in the afternoon light, her pale dress glimmering among the dark firs, while Marian remained at the edge of the trees where she could see without being seen. Ahead of her, the old boathouse stood silent and half hidden at the water's edge, and its dark windows seemed to watch her approach.

Inside the dim boathouse, Anne waited in her white dress, her thin hands twisting nervously together. When the two women stood face to face in the green half-light, the likeness was so startling that Laura felt she was looking into a mirror, though a darker and sadder one than any she had known. Anne gazed at her in silence for a long moment, and then whispered that she saw Mrs Fairlie's own face in hers.

Anne told Laura, in a hurried whisper, that Sir Percival had a secret so terrible that it could ruin his name and his position if it were ever made known. Her own mother knew it too, she said, and had helped to hide it years ago, and it was only because Anne herself had guessed the truth that Sir Percival had locked her away in the asylum. She trembled as she spoke, like a bird that has flown too near a cage.

At last Anne offered to tell Laura everything, on one condition: that Laura should promise to keep it from every living soul. Laura, who had never kept a secret from her sister, answered gently that she could not make such a promise without knowing what it meant. Anne hesitated, looked about her with wide frightened eyes, and seemed to be struggling with some inner terror.

Suddenly a long shadow slid across the wall of the boathouse, and Anne sprang to her feet with a cry of terror. She whispered that someone had been listening, snatched up her shawl and fled into the dark woods before Laura could speak, and in a moment the white figure had vanished among the trees. Marian, who had run forward at the sound, saw only a tall, broad shape disappearing in the direction of the house.

That evening Sir Percival, who had been told of the meeting by Madame Fosco, caught Laura roughly by the arm in the hall and demanded to know every word that Anne Catherick had said. His face was dark with anger and, Marian thought, with something even worse, which looked remarkably like fear. Laura answered in a trembling voice that she would tell him nothing, since he had never told her why Anne had been shut away.

Marian wrenched Sir Percival's hand from Laura's arm and placed herself between them like a shield, glaring at him with all her strength. At that moment the Count entered the hall, and with a few smooth words and a gentle hand on his friend's shoulder, he turned the storm aside once again. Marian realised, with a shiver, that the Count was the one person in the house whom Sir Percival feared, and that this made him more dangerous than any shout.

Sir Percival sent his men through the woods and fields with lanterns, and he questioned the farmers and the villagers for miles around, but Anne had vanished without leaving a trace. Marian understood that her sister's husband was frightened by something, and that the Count, who watched everything with a smile, was somehow part of it. She resolved that she would discover what the two men were planning, even if she had to listen at doors to do it.

One heavy, thundery night Marian saw a light in the library and heard the low murmur of men's voices on the terrace below her bedroom window. Forgetting every rule of what a lady should do, she climbed out onto the sloping roof of the veranda, where she lay flat on the warm slates and held her breath. Above her the sky was black with cloud, and the air hung over the house like a lid.

Lying on the cold slates with her ear close to the edge, Marian heard Sir Percival speak in a hoarse and desperate voice about the money he owed. His creditors would not wait any longer, he said, and unless he found a large sum within a few weeks he would lose his house, his name and his freedom. The Count listened with a soothing murmur, like a doctor listening to a patient who cannot be cured.

The Count replied, in his gentlest and most reasonable tone, that Lady Glyde's money could still be obtained, if only they were patient and clever, and that something must be devised. Sir Percival said hurriedly, almost in a whisper, that there must be no violence, whatever happened, and the Count answered with a soft laugh that a man of his experience would never dream of it. That soft and comfortable laughter went through Marian like a cold blade, and she pressed her face against the wet slates to keep from crying out.

As Marian lay listening, the two men began to speak about Anne Catherick, and she caught the words that this woman was extraordinarily like Lady Glyde, and that she was ill and weak. Then the wind began to rise in the firs, rustling and moaning around the house, and the rest of their conversation was carried away into the darkness. Marian dug her nails into her palms in frustration, for she knew that she had heard something of the greatest importance without understanding it.

All at once the storm broke with a flash and a roar, and the rain came down in sheets upon the roof, soaking Marian to the skin in a few minutes. She dared not move while the men were still talking beneath her, and so she lay there for what seemed like hours, shivering with cold and fear, until at last they went indoors and she could creep back. Her limbs were so stiff that she could hardly lift herself over the sill.

When the men had finally gone indoors, Marian crept back through her window, so numb that she fell onto the carpet and lay there for some moments gasping for breath. She tore off her wet clothes and wrapped herself in a shawl, but she could not get warm, and she felt a strange heat beginning to rise in her head. She knew that she was in danger, yet she could think of nothing but the need to write down what she had heard.

By the light of a single guttering candle, Marian opened her diary and wrote down every word she could remember of the terrible conversation. Her hand trembled so badly that the pen skidded across the page, but she forced herself to go on until she had set down the warning that Laura must be protected. At last the pen fell from her fingers, and her head sank forward onto the paper.

In the morning Laura came to her sister's room and found her lying across the bed, burning with fever and murmuring words that made no sense. A servant was sent at once to the village for the doctor, Mr Dawson, and Laura, white with fright, sat down beside the bed and bathed her sister's face with cool water. She had never seen Marian helpless, and the sight frightened her more than all of Sir Percival's anger.

Mr Dawson shook his head gravely and said that the fever was very serious, and that it might last for many days. The Count and Madame Fosco came to the bedside with expressions of deep concern and offered to help with the nursing, and Laura, who was too anxious and too tired to doubt anyone, accepted their kindness with tears of gratitude. It seemed to her that Providence had sent them to Blackwater at the right moment.

For many nights Laura kept watch beside her sister's bed, bathing her face and listening to the broken words that came from her lips in the fever. The great house fell silent, as though it were holding its breath, and no sound was heard but the ticking of the clock and the distant noise of the wind in the trees. Laura, exhausted and frightened, did not understand that she was being slowly separated from the only friend she had in the world.

One night, while Marian tossed and muttered in her fever, the Count stepped into her room with the soft tread of a cat. His quick eye found the corner of her diary under her pillow, and with his large and delicate hand he drew it out, smiling as though he had found a treasure. The whole household was asleep, and no one saw him carry the little book to the candle.

The Count settled himself in a chair and read the diary from beginning to end, nodding and smiling at the cleverest passages like a connoisseur at a play. He learned from it everything that Marian knew, everything that she feared and everything she had overheard on the roof, and he found that her mind was more acute than he had expected. When he reached her last, trembling lines, he sighed with something like genuine admiration.

Before he left the room, the Count took her pen and wrote a long and graceful note at the end of the diary in his own bold hand, praising her courage, her intelligence and her sisterly devotion. He signed it with a flourish, replaced the little book under her pillow and withdrew without a sound, as satisfied as an artist who has added a signature to a masterpiece. Not a single soul in the sleeping house suspected what had happened under its roof that night.

Within a few days Sir Percival suddenly dismissed nearly all his servants, saying that he must save money, and Mrs Michelson herself was sent off to the seaside for a holiday. The great house, which had never been cheerful, became bare and echoing, and only the Count, his wife and a few remaining servants walked its empty corridors. Laura could not shake off the feeling that she was being shut inside a trap.

Laura begged to be allowed to sit with her sister again, but the Count, with every show of concern, declared that the room was dangerous and that she must save her strength. In desperation she wrote to Mr Fairlie, asking him to come and fetch her, and put the letter in the hall for the post, but it vanished and no answer ever came. She felt that an invisible wall was rising around her, and that she had nobody to turn to.

At last the fever broke, and Marian woke, thin as a ghost and so weak that she could not lift her head from the pillow. Under it she found her diary, and, turning the pages with her feeble fingers, she came upon the Count's long note in his flowing hand and understood that he had read all her secrets. The shock made her heart pound, for she realised that he knew exactly what she knew, and that he would act accordingly.

Mr Dawson declared that the worst was over and that Marian was now out of danger, though she must have complete rest. The Count suggested, with the sweetest solicitude, that the clean, bracing air of Cumberland would restore her faster than any physic, and that she should be sent to Limmeridge as soon as she could bear the journey. Mr Dawson, who suspected nothing, thought it an excellent idea, and the arrangements were made that very afternoon.

A few days later Marian was lifted into a carriage with a nurse beside her, still far too weak to argue or to stand. As the horses drew away from the house, she looked back and saw Laura waving from an upstairs window, small and pale against the dark stone, and a terrible fear for her sister squeezed her heart. She tried to cry out that Laura should not be left alone, but her voice was no more than a whisper.

After Marian's departure, the Count came to Laura with a grave face and told her that her sister had been too weak to travel farther than London. She was resting in his own house there, he said, and begged Laura to come to her at once, and Sir Percival added that it was a very proper thing to do. Laura, who longed to see Marian again and had no reason to doubt such a kind message, agreed immediately.

The next day Laura left Blackwater Park alone, drove to the station and took the train to London, glad to be leaving the gloomy house behind her. As the green fields and little villages slid past the carriage window, she thought of how happy she would be to see Marian again, and how safe she would feel. She did not know that every step she took was being carried out according to a plan.

Meanwhile, in London, Anne Catherick had fallen seriously ill, for her heart had always been weak and the long strain of fear had worn her out. She had travelled to the city in the company of her old friend Mrs Clements, but the noise and the crowds had been more than she could bear. She lay in a small plain room, pale and trembling, with no idea that powerful enemies were drawing close.

The Count and his wife, who had been watching for Anne, found her in her sickness and carried her off to their house in St John's Wood. She was too weak and bewildered to resist, and she was helped up the stairs and laid in a bed in an upper room, with the curtains drawn against the daylight. In the house below, the cook, Hester Pinhorn, was told that the poor lady upstairs was Lady Glyde, and that she was dangerously ill.

During the night, on the twenty-fifth of July, Anne Catherick died quietly of the weak heart she had carried all her life. The doctor who was called to the house had been told that the sick lady was Lady Glyde, and he wrote that name upon the certificate without a doubt in his mind. Thus, on paper, the wife of Sir Percival Glyde was dead, though the real Lady Glyde was still alive and travelling toward London.

The next day Laura's train came steaming into the London station, and there on the platform stood the Count, immense and smiling, with his hat in his hand. He bowed low, declared that her sister was waiting for her with every kindness, and handed her into a cab as carefully as if she were made of glass. She smiled with relief, and did not see the look that passed over his face.

The cab rolled through the crowded streets of London to the Count's house in St John's Wood, where Madame Fosco received Laura in the hall with a cold and formal smile. Laura looked eagerly around for Marian, but her sister was nowhere to be seen, and Madame Fosco said smoothly that Miss Halcombe had gone out for a little air and would soon return. Laura, tired and anxious after the long journey, sat down in the drawing room to wait for her sister to come back.

Madame Fosco poured out a cup of tea and pressed it upon Laura with a kind word, and Laura drank it gratefully. It had a strange taste, and within minutes the room began to swim before her eyes, her hands grew numb and a heavy sleepiness fell upon her like a net. She tried to rise and call for help, but her knees gave way, and she sank into darkness.

When Laura woke, she found herself in a bare room, dressed in plain clothes marked with the name Anne Catherick, and her own dress and jewels were gone. A hard-faced woman, who gave her name as Mrs Rubelle, told her that she was Anne Catherick, an escaped patient, and that she was to be taken back to the asylum at once. Laura cried out that she was Lady Glyde, and that this was a terrible mistake, but nobody listened.

A closed carriage was waiting at the door, and Laura was led down the stairs between two firm women, whose grip upon her arms was gentle but impossible to break. She said again and again that she was Lady Glyde and that her husband would pay for this outrage, but they merely shook their heads and murmured that all the patients said such things. The blinds were drawn down tight, and the heavy carriage rolled away through the noisy streets toward some unknown and dreadful place.

At the gate of the asylum a doctor received Laura as though he had been expecting Anne Catherick all along, and he checked her description against the papers brought by the nurse. When she cried that she was really Lady Glyde, he smiled with practised kindness and wrote a note in his book, recording that the patient was suffering from the old delusion that she was a great lady. The heavy door closed behind her with a hollow sound that seemed to cut her off from everything she had ever known.

Day after day Laura lived among strangers in the asylum, in a bare room with high windows, wearing the plain white dress that had been given to her. The nurses were kind but firm, and every time she insisted that she was Lady Glyde, they smiled and made a note that the delusion had returned. She began to fear that, if she went on protesting, she might truly lose her reason.

A few days later a letter with a broad black edge arrived at Limmeridge House, and Mr Fairlie, who opened it with a trembling hand, was struck speechless. It announced that Lady Glyde had died suddenly in London, at the house of Count Fosco, of a disease of the heart, and that the doctor's certificate was enclosed. Marian, still pale from her illness, took the paper from her uncle's fingers and read it twice without believing a word.

Marian was overcome with grief and horror, and she stood at the window with her hands pressed against the glass, unable to speak or to weep. Mr Fairlie, on the other hand, wept loudly and at length, but he complained still more bitterly about the damage that such a blow had done to his delicate nerves. It seemed to Marian that the kindest thing she could do was to leave the room, and she went out into the garden to be alone.

Sir Percival wrote that his wife was to be laid to rest beside her mother in the family vault at Limmeridge, and the necessary arrangements were made at once. A black hearse brought the coffin north by road, and the villagers stood bareheaded along the lane as it passed, for every one of them had loved the sweet-faced girl who had grown up among them. Marian watched it from the steps of the house with burning eyes, still unable to cry.

The funeral took place on a grey, windless morning, and many of the villagers wept openly as the coffin was lowered into the vault beside Mrs Fairlie's tomb. Sir Percival did not come, and Mr Fairlie, who could not bear the sight of mourning, stayed in his room, so that Marian stood almost alone at the grave. The marble above it was afterward cut with the name of Laura, Lady Glyde, and the date that the doctor had given.

When the mourners had gone, Marian remained beside the tomb, resting her hand on the cold white marble and staring at the freshly cut name. It was strange, but she could not feel that Laura lay beneath it, and a small, stubborn voice in the back of her mind kept insisting that there was something wrong with the whole story. She stayed there until the light faded, and went home with that voice still speaking.

That night Marian took out her diary and read it again, page by page, until she came once more to the Count's long and flattering note. Slowly she began to see how carefully he had planned each step, and how neatly she had been put out of the way at the very moment when Laura needed her most. The memory of that soft laughter on the terrace returned to her, and she knew that the Count was capable of anything.

A few days later Mrs Clements, Anne's old friend, arrived at Limmeridge in a state of great distress, having travelled all the way from London in search of help. She told Marian that Anne had been taken ill, that she had left her for a short time, and that when she came back, Anne had gone, leaving no message and no trace. She had searched the streets and the hospitals for days, and she was now almost out of her mind with worry.

Marian listened to Mrs Clements with a growing and dreadful excitement, for the dates seemed to fit together in a way that could not be a coincidence. Anne had vanished from London at almost the very moment when Lady Glyde was said to have died there, and the two women had been so alike that no stranger could have told them apart. It dawned on her that the woman in the tomb might be Anne Catherick, and that Laura might still be alive.

Marian said nothing of her suspicions to Mr Fairlie, who would only have been annoyed, and instead she packed a small bag and travelled to London at once with Mrs Clements. They went straight to the Count's house in St John's Wood, but they found it shut and empty, with the Count, his wife and every servant gone. The neighbours could say only that a closed carriage had driven away from the door some days before.

Mrs Clements remembered the name of the asylum from which Anne had escaped long before, and it seemed to Marian the likeliest place in which to begin her search. They went to the gates together, and Marian, speaking with all the calm she could summon, asked whether a new patient had been brought there in a closed carriage within the last few days. The porter, a heavy man with a suspicious face, looked at her for a long moment before he gave any answer at all.

The porter refused to answer a single one of Marian's questions, and when she asked to see the doctor, she was told that he was engaged and could receive nobody. A message came back, in the end, that visitors were not allowed and that the asylum could give no information whatever about its patients. Marian walked away from the gate with her face set, resolving that she would find another way.

Marian waited in the lane beside the high wall until a nurse came out on an errand, and she offered the woman a sum of money for a few minutes of honest talk. The nurse, who had been struck by the new patient's gentle manner, admitted that a woman had been brought in some days before, in the clothes of Anne Catherick, who kept insisting that she was Lady Glyde. Marian's heart gave a great leap, and she had to hold on to the wall.

The nurse explained that the patients were allowed to walk in the walled garden every evening at dusk, and for a larger sum she agreed to let Marian into a corner where she could watch without being seen. Marian stood in the shadow of a tall hedge, hardly daring to breathe, while the pale figures drifted past her in the fading light. Then, at the end of the line, came a thin, fair woman in a plain white dress, walking with her head bowed.

Marian stepped out from behind the hedge, and as the thin woman raised her head, she saw to her unspeakable joy that it was Laura, pale and changed but alive. For a moment Laura stared at her like someone waking from a long and terrible dream, and then she whispered her sister's name and fell weeping into her arms. The nurse, standing a little way off, turned her back and pretended to see nothing.

Marian could not bear to leave Laura inside those walls for a single further night, and she whispered a plan to the nurse in the shadow of a doorway. In return for a large payment, the woman promised to unlock a side door in the garden wall at midnight and to lead Laura out through it, while Marian would wait with a cab at the end of the lane. Both of them knew that if they were caught, Laura would never be free again.

At midnight Marian stood in the dark lane beside the hired cab, wrapped in a heavy cloak, her eyes fixed upon the high wall and her ears straining for the slightest sound. The night was cold and still, a distant clock struck the quarter hours, and every minute seemed as long as an hour. Beside her, Mrs Clements prayed under her breath, and the horse stamped patiently in the shadows.

At last, a little after midnight, a small door opened in the wall, and the nurse thrust Laura out into the lane with a whispered word and a push. Marian caught her in her arms before she could fall, and the door closed again with a dull click, as though it had never been opened at all. Laura was trembling and could scarcely stand, and she looked at the open night with the eyes of a child.

Marian and Mrs Clements lifted Laura into the cab between them and wrapped her in a rug, and the driver, who had been well paid, whipped up the horse and set off through the empty streets. No sound of pursuit followed them, no lamp flashed behind them, and little by little the tall black wall sank out of sight. Laura sat in Marian's arms with her eyes closed, and for the first time in many days her breathing was calm.

Laura slept for almost a whole day in the small lodgings that Marian had found, and when she woke, she told her sister everything, though with many gaps. She remembered the cup of tea, the heavy darkness, the strange room, the clothes marked with Anne's name and the cold voices telling her that she was someone else. Marian listened with her hands clenched, and her horror grew as the story unfolded.

Marian had very little money left, and Laura's mind was still clouded and confused, so that she often forgot where she was and sometimes even who she had been. Sitting beside her sleeping sister, Marian made a solemn promise that nobody would ever take her away again, though she did not yet know how it could be done. She thought of Walter Hartright, so far away across the sea, and wished with all her heart that he were at hand.

After many months of fever, hardship and danger in the forests of Central America, Walter at last sailed for home, thin, brown and much older than the young man who had left. He had come close to death more than once, and the long suffering had taught him a good deal about courage, but it had not made him forget Laura. As the English coast rose out of the grey sea, his heart beat faster than it had done in all his journeys.

Walter went straight to Hampstead, where his mother and his sister Sarah welcomed him with tears of joy and a table loaded with food. But when, as casually as he could, he asked for news of Limmeridge, the two women exchanged a troubled look, and at last his sister told him gently that Lady Glyde was dead.
