The words struck Walter like a physical blow, and for a long time he could not speak.

Walter travelled north as fast as the trains would carry him, and went from the station directly to the little churchyard at Limmeridge. There, beside the old tomb of Mrs Fairlie, stood the fresh white marble with its new inscription, and he read the name of Laura, Lady Glyde, through eyes blurred with tears. He sank down on the grass beside it, and for a long time he sat in silence, unable to think.

As Walter sat there, two women in long black veils came through the churchyard gate and walked slowly toward the tomb. Unwilling to be seen in his sorrow, he drew back behind the trunk of a great yew tree and waited for them to pass, though he could not help watching them. One of them was tall and walked with the free stride of a woman of character, while the other leaned heavily upon her arm.

Beside the tomb, the leaning woman raised her veil, and Walter, looking out from behind the tree, saw a face that he knew better than his own. For a moment he thought that he was seeing a ghost, or that the sun and his own grief had deceived him, but the figure was moving, breathing and real. It was Laura, thinner and paler than she had been before, but undoubtedly alive, and Walter felt the ground shake beneath his feet.

Walter stepped out from behind the tree, and Marian, lifting her own veil, cried out aloud at the sight of him as though he were the answer to a prayer. Laura looked at him slowly, with a puzzled and gentle expression, like someone trying to remember a face from a dream. Then her lips moved, and she said his name in a whisper, and his heart nearly broke with joy and pity.

Marian told Walter the whole terrible story in low, quick words as they stood among the gravestones, from the dinner at Blackwater Park to the midnight escape from the asylum. Walter learned with horror that the woman who lay beneath the white marble was not Laura at all, but poor Anne Catherick, who had died in the Count's house and been buried under another's name. He listened with clenched fists and a darkening face, and his anger against the two conspirators grew with every word.

Walter brought the two women back with him to London and found them a set of small, cheap rooms in a quiet street not far from his own lodgings. The rooms were poor and plainly furnished, but there they were hidden among thousands of strangers, where neither Sir Percival nor the Count was likely to look. Walter paid the first month's rent himself, and he said that they must not worry about money, because he would earn enough for all three of them.

The three lived quietly together on very little money, and each of them did what he or she could to help. Marian took in needlework, Laura slowly began to draw again, and Walter worked long hours late into the night, selling his sketches and engravings to any dealer who would pay for them. In the midst of their poverty there was a kind of happiness, for they were together and they trusted each other completely.

One evening Walter stood before the two sisters in the little room and made a solemn promise, in a voice that shook with feeling. He swore that he would prove who Laura really was, restore her name and her place in the world, and make Sir Percival and the Count answer for what they had done. Laura looked at him with tears in her eyes, and Marian said quietly that she would help him with every ounce of her strength.

Walter went to the office of a London lawyer named Mr Kyrle, a grave and careful man, and laid the whole extraordinary story before him. The lawyer listened with his fingertips pressed together, interrupting only to ask short, sharp questions about names, dates and places. When Walter had finished, Mr Kyrle sat for some time in silence, looking at the papers on his desk.

Mr Kyrle said at last that he believed every word, but that belief was not the same thing as proof, and the law demanded proof of the strongest kind. A doctor's certificate, a funeral, a tomb and the testimony of a whole family all said that Lady Glyde was dead, and a woman who denied it could easily be called mad. He added, with real sorrow, that without more evidence no court in England would listen to them.

Mr Kyrle tapped the calendar on his desk and said that the date on the death certificate might be the weak point in the whole conspiracy. If they could prove that Lady Glyde had been alive and well after the day on which she was said to have died, then the certificate must be false, and everything built upon it would fall. The difficulty, he said, was that such proof was hard to find, and that Sir Percival and the Count would surely deny it.

That evening Walter asked Laura, as gently as he could, about the day when she had left Blackwater Park and travelled to London. She remembered the train, the green fields and the Count's smile on the platform, but the exact day and the date were lost in the mist that still clouded her mind, and she began to weep with frustration. Walter took her hand and told her not to trouble, since there were other ways to find out.

Walter paid a visit to Mrs Clements, who dried her eyes with her apron and told him all she knew about Anne's last days. She described how the poor creature had fallen ill in London, how a strange lady had called at the lodgings, and how, when she herself had gone out for a short time, she had returned to find the room empty. She had never seen Anne again, she said, and the thought made her heart ache.

Mrs Clements added that Anne had often spoken of her mother and of the village of Welmingham in Hampshire, where Mrs Catherick had lived in former days. Anne had always believed, without being able to say why, that Sir Percival's secret had something to do with the old church in that village. Walter wrote the name down carefully, as a drowning man might seize a rope.

Walter tracked down Hester Pinhorn, the cook who had worked for the Count in St John's Wood, and she told him, with a good deal of nervous hesitation, what she had seen. A sick lady had been carried upstairs and had died during the night of the twenty-fifth of July, and she had been told that it was Lady Glyde, though she herself had never seen the lady well. Hester said that she would gladly repeat her story in front of a judge.

Walter laid the dates side by side and saw with a leap of the heart that the certificate could not be true. Anne had died on the twenty-fifth of July, but from the day of Marian's own journey north Walter worked out that Laura had set out for London only on the twenty-sixth, a whole day after her supposed death. Mr Kyrle was pleased with this discovery, yet he warned Walter that a single date, without witnesses, would never be enough.

Walter and Marian talked until late at night, and they agreed that the one weapon they still lacked was Sir Percival's secret. If they could discover what Anne Catherick had guessed, and what her mother had helped to conceal, they might force the baronet to confess to the plot, and so to restore Laura. Laura, who had listened in silence, said softly that she remembered Anne speaking of a church book.

Early the next morning Walter said goodbye to Marian, and to Laura, who pressed a small keepsake into his hand and told him to come back safely. He walked to the station through the grey streets, feeling lighter than he had for many months, because for the first time he had something to do, and a place in which to do it. The train carried him south toward the village of Welmingham and the old church that might hold the secret.

Walter reached the village of Welmingham in Hampshire at the end of a long, hot day, tired and dusty from the train and the road. It was a very quiet place, with low cottages, wide green fields and an old grey church standing at one end of the single street. He stood for a while in the shade of its tower, wondering what secrets such a peaceful spot could possibly hold.

At the church door Walter met the parish clerk, a wrinkled old man who leaned on a stick, was nearly deaf and loved to talk even more than he loved to listen. He was delighted to have a visitor in a place where visitors were rare, and he agreed with great pleasure to show Walter everything the old building contained. Walter had to shout each of his questions twice before the clerk understood them.

The old clerk unlocked a small door beside the altar and led Walter into the vestry, a cramped, dim room that smelled of dust and candle wax. Against the wall stood a heavy iron press, and in it, row upon row, lay the parish registers in which every marriage, birth and burial in the village had been written for generations. The clerk patted the iron door proudly and said that no book had ever been lost from it.

Walter asked the clerk whether he could look at the register that recorded the marriage of Sir Felix Glyde, the father of Sir Percival, and the old man fetched it with many remarks about the glories of the past. Walter turned the heavy yellow pages until at last his finger stopped at an entry that declared Sir Felix and his lady to have been married in that very church. It was the proof that Sir Percival needed, written out in a clear and careful hand.

Holding the book close to the lamp, Walter noticed that the ink of this entry was fresher than that of its neighbours, and that its lines were crowded into too small a space. It looked as though the writer had squeezed the words between two older entries, long after the pages around them had been filled. A suspicion, small and cold, began to stir in the back of Walter's mind, and he did not dare to put it into words.

Without a word to the clerk, who had dozed off in his chair in the warm air, Walter copied the entry carefully, letter for letter, onto a sheet of paper from his pocket. As he wrote, his suspicion hardened into certainty, for the more he looked at the entry the more it seemed to him the work of some other hand than the clerk of that time. If it was a forgery, then Sir Percival's whole name rested upon a lie.

When the clerk woke, he began to chatter about the old days, and he spoke of a Mr Catherick, who had been clerk before him and had kept the vestry key on his own person. Mr Catherick's wife, he added with a shake of the head, had once been the talk of the whole village, and had gone away in disgrace, though he understood that she now lived in Southampton in great respectability. Walter noted every word with care, and understood that he must go and see this woman for himself, whatever it might cost him.

Walter took the next train to Southampton and asked his way through the busy streets to the home of Mrs Catherick, which stood in a quiet row of tidy houses. It was a neat little dwelling with spotless windows and a brass knocker polished like a mirror, and everything about it seemed to proclaim the owner's determination to be respectable. Walter knocked at the door, and a maidservant took his name to her mistress, and left him to wait in the narrow hall.

Mrs Catherick received Walter in her immaculate parlour, sitting bolt upright in her chair with her chin lifted and her hands folded, a proud, stern woman who seemed to have turned herself into stone. She told him in a flat voice that Sir Percival Glyde had always been a most generous friend to her, and that she would not tolerate a word against him in her house. Walter, studying her cold face and her hard eyes, felt quite certain that she was hiding something of the greatest importance.

When Walter pressed her about her daughter, Mrs Catherick's composure cracked at last, and she turned on him with flashing eyes, saying that he would never learn what he sought to know. In the heat of her anger she let slip the sentence that the man whom Walter was pursuing had no real right to his name or to his title, and then she clamped her lips shut in dismay. Walter bowed, thanked her politely and left, knowing that he had learned all that he needed.

As soon as Walter had gone, Mrs Catherick sat down at her little desk and wrote a hurried letter to Sir Percival Glyde, her hand shaking with alarm. She warned him that a young man had visited her, that he had asked about Anne and about the church at Welmingham, and that he seemed to know a great deal more than he ought. She sealed the letter with a heavy heart, for she knew exactly what it would set in motion.

Back in London, Walter told Marian and Laura everything he had found at Welmingham and Southampton, and Marian's eyes lit up with fierce hope. That same evening Pesca came by with an invitation to the opera, declaring that a man who worked so hard should be refreshed by music. Walter, who badly needed an evening's rest from his anxieties, accepted gladly, and they set out together for the theatre.

In the middle of the first act, Pesca suddenly turned as white as paper and fixed his eyes on a huge, calm, smiling man who sat in a box on the other side of the theatre. His whole small body began to tremble, and he clutched Walter's arm so hard that it hurt, whispering in Italian words that Walter could not follow. The music rolled on, and the great man in the box beat time on the edge of it with a plump hand.

In the corridor outside, Pesca whispered, in a trembling voice, that the huge man was a spy and a traitor to a secret Italian society known as the Brotherhood, of which Pesca himself had long been a member. He had known the traitor in Italy under another name, he said, and he knew that a man who betrayed the Brotherhood had no safe place left on earth. If the traitor saw him here, Pesca added, they might both be in the gravest danger.

At that moment the huge man looked across the theatre and met Pesca's eyes, and for an instant his smiling face seemed to turn to stone. He rose slowly and gracefully from his seat and left the box, and Walter, remembering all that Marian had told him, understood with a rush of excitement that this was Count Fosco himself. Pesca, by his side, had begun to shake from head to foot as if he were in a fever, and he begged Walter to take him home at once.

Walter had the uneasy feeling that Mrs Catherick would already have warned Sir Percival, and that the baronet would try to destroy the register before the truth could be proved. He hurried back to Hampshire by the night train, and in the dark he took up a position among the gravestones, where he could watch the church without being seen. The village was asleep, and the only sound was the whisper of the wind in the yew trees.

Late that night, a hurrying figure came along the lane to the church, and Walter saw by the light of the moon that it was Sir Percival Glyde himself, carrying a lantern. He opened the vestry door with a key which, as it later proved, he had had secretly made, and slipped inside, closing the door behind him. Walter's heart began to pound, for he saw that the baronet had come exactly as he had feared.

Inside the vestry Sir Percival opened the register, found the page he sought and tore it out with fierce, trembling hands, and then he set his lantern down upon a shelf of old papers. The dry sheets caught at once, and in a moment the little room was full of crackling flame and choking smoke, while the heavy door, which had locked behind him, would not open. He pounded upon it with his fists, and his cries rose above the roar.

Bells began to ring, and the villagers came running toward the burning church with buckets and ladders, shouting to one another in the red light. Walter flung himself at the vestry door together with the old clerk, and again and again they tried to break it open, while from within came Sir Percival's desperate cries. The flames roared higher, and the smoke rolled out so thick that the rescuers were driven back, choking and half blind.

When the flames had at last died down, the body of Sir Percival Glyde was found in the ruined vestry, and the coroner, after hearing the witnesses, decided that his death had been an accident. Walter, who had wanted him to answer before a court for his crimes, took no triumph in his end, only a heavy sadness at the waste of a human life. The register was burned, but his own careful copy of the entry was safe in his pocket.

Walter soon discovered where Count Fosco was lodging, in a quiet and respectable street not far from the river, and the next morning he climbed the narrow staircase to the Count's rooms. His heart was beating fast, for he knew that he was about to face the cleverest man he had ever met, and that everything depended on this one meeting. At the top of the stairs, he knocked firmly and was told in a deep voice to come in.

The Count received him with perfect politeness, rising from his enormous chair among the cages of birds and the family of white mice that still shared his lodging. Walter told him plainly that he knew about the plot against Lady Glyde, the substitution of Anne Catherick and the false certificate of death, and he spoke without raising his voice. The Count heard him out with a courteous smile, and then shook his head sorrowfully and said that Walter must be dreaming.

Walter said quietly that his friend Pesca had recognised the Count at the opera, and knew him as a traitor to the secret society called the Brotherhood. For the first time since the interview began, the great calm face lost its colour, and the smile faded from the Count's lips like a lamp being put out. He sat down heavily in his chair, and the little mice squeaked in their cage.

Walter proposed a bargain, which the Count, after a long and thoughtful silence, found that he could not refuse. If the Count would write out a full and truthful confession of the plot against Lady Glyde, Walter would stay silent for a few hours, so that the Count might leave England before the Brotherhood could learn where he was. The Count bowed his huge head in agreement, like a man accepting a sentence.

Throughout the long night the Count sat at a large table in the lamplight and wrote, quickly and elegantly, with a white mouse perched upon his shoulder and a cup of black coffee at his elbow. Now and then he paused to joke gently about his own cleverness, or to praise the courage of Miss Halcombe, whose diary he had read with such enjoyment. Walter sat in a chair across from him and watched every line as it appeared.

Madame Fosco sat bolt upright in a corner of the room throughout the night, never speaking a word and never taking her eyes off her husband for more than a moment. Walter, who had thought her as guilty as the Count himself, began to see in her face a deep and terrible devotion that left no room for fear or conscience. It was a strange sight, and he found, to his surprise, that he felt a kind of pity for her.

As the Count finished each page, Walter took it and read it, and he saw the whole plot laid out before him with chilling clearness. It described how Anne Catherick had died in the Count's house, how her death had been used to bury Lady Glyde's name, and how Laura had been tricked, drugged and sent to the asylum as Anne. The Count had told everything with the pride of an artist, and without a trace of shame.

The confession was exact in every detail of time and place, and Walter found with delight that it set down all the important dates. According to the Count's own hand, Anne Catherick had died on the twenty-fifth of July, while Laura had reached London alive and well on the twenty-sixth, so that the certificate of death was proved false by its own author. This was the very proof that Mr Kyrle had said they must find, and Walter read the sentence three times to be sure that he was not dreaming.

At dawn the Count wrote the last words, signed his name with a magnificent flourish and handed the whole bundle of pages to Walter with a polite and gracious bow. He said, with perfect sincerity, that he admired Walter's courage and persistence, and that it was a pleasure to have been beaten by an honourable opponent. Then he turned to his wife and spoke a few quiet words in Italian, and she rose silently to pack.

Walter carried the confession home through the grey streets of early morning, holding the pages close against his chest, as though they were made of gold. He had promised to say nothing for a few hours, and he kept his word to the letter, although he loathed the man to whom he had given it. In the little room in which Marian and Laura waited, he laid the papers upon the table, and for a while no one spoke.

Marian and Laura read the Count's pages together at the little table, and Marian's face darkened as she came to the passages where he praised his own cleverness. Yet her anger was mixed with a fierce hope, for she saw that here, in the very handwriting of the man who had ruined them, lay the proof they had so long been seeking. Laura, who understood only a part of it, held Walter's hand and said nothing.

The Count and his wife left London the same day, and a steamer carried them over the grey sea to France, with their birds and their mice in a covered cage beside them. Walter kept his promise to the letter and told no one for many hours, although he longed to let Pesca know at once where the traitor had gone. He felt that a promise given even to an enemy was still a promise, and that his own honour was worth more than a few hours' revenge.

Some weeks later, Walter noticed a short paragraph in a newspaper that told of an unknown man, of enormous size, who had been found dead in a street in Paris and had not yet been identified. Something in the description made his heart stop, for he remembered the vast calm figure among the cages and the mice. He put on his hat and took the next boat to France to see for himself, because he could not bear to leave the matter in doubt.

At the Paris morgue, among the silent rows of the unknown dead, Walter saw the vast body of Count Fosco lying quite still, with a calm and almost noble expression on his face. On the arm there was a small red mark of the kind that Pesca had once described to him, and Walter understood that the Brotherhood had found its traitor at last and put him to death. He stood for a moment with bowed head, and then turned away without a word.

Back in London, Walter told Pesca briefly what he had seen in the morgue, and the little Italian sat silent for a long time with his hands over his face. At last he asked, in a low voice, that Walter should never speak of the Brotherhood or of what had happened in Paris to anyone as long as he lived. Walter gave his word, and neither of the friends ever mentioned the matter again.

Mr Kyrle read the Count's confession twice through, slowly, and when he laid it down, his face wore its first look of real satisfaction. He said that it was very strong evidence, since the guilty man had set down the dates himself, but he advised Walter to gather as many witnesses as possible, so that no doubt should remain. A case of this size and seriousness, he said, must be built as carefully and as solidly as a wall of iron, brick by brick.

Walter found Mrs Michelson, the housekeeper of Blackwater Park, and Hester Pinhorn, the cook from St John's Wood, and persuaded both women to sign statements in the lawyer's office. Mrs Michelson described the quarrels over the paper, the dismissal of the servants and the day on which Lady Glyde had left for London, while Hester told of the sick lady and the night of the twenty-fifth. Between them, the two accounts fitted together like the pieces of a broken plate.

Marian sat for many evenings copying out the pages of her diary, including the long note that the Count had added in his own bold handwriting, so that all might be kept safely as evidence. The diary showed, entry after entry, what had been planned at Blackwater Park, how Sir Percival had pressed for money and how the Count had managed him. Marian found a grim satisfaction in thinking that the Count's own flourish would help to condemn him.

Mr Kyrle said at last that the best evidence of all would be Laura's own face, shown in the place where she had been born. If the tenants and the villagers of Limmeridge, who had known her from childhood, would recognise and welcome her, then her uncle could not deny her, nor could the law refuse to hear the case. He added that all the papers should go with them, in case Mr Fairlie made difficulties.

The three of them travelled north together by train, with the precious box of papers on the seat beside Walter, while the mist lifted from the fields and a pale sun came out. Laura seemed clearer in her mind than she had been for many months, and she looked out of the window at the hills with a quiet and growing interest, as though old memories were waking within her. Marian pressed her hand, and Walter felt that the long struggle was nearly over.

When the carriage reached the village of Limmeridge, the news ran from door to door, and the villagers and tenants came hurrying into the lane to see for themselves. They knew Laura at once, in spite of her thin face and her plain dress, and many of the old women wept openly with joy while the men took off their hats and shouted. Laura, with tears running down her cheeks, shook hand after hand and called each person by name, and every doubt was swept away.

The tenants followed Laura all the way up the drive to Limmeridge House, cheering and waving their hats, and the servants came running out onto the steps to see what the noise could mean. Marian took her sister's arm and led her up through the open door into the hall where she had played as a child, while the old servants stood back in amazement. Walter followed with the box of papers, feeling that he had never been so proud.

In his darkened room Mr Fairlie, wrapped in his shawl, at first refused to believe that the young woman before him could be his niece, since belief would have meant a great deal of trouble. Walter laid the Count's confession and the sworn statements upon the table one by one, and the sound of the cheering tenants beneath the window showed the old man that he could not possibly deny her. His thin hand began to tremble, and his lip began to shake, and the whole room waited in silence for what he would say.

At last Mr Fairlie gave way with a long sigh, and in a trembling hand signed the paper that acknowledged Laura as his niece and the true Lady Glyde. He complained loudly that the whole affair had been very bad for his nerves, and that he ought to have been spared such a shock, but nobody in the room took the least notice. Marian, looking at him with something between pity and contempt, was content to let him have the last word.

In the churchyard, a mason cut away the false inscription from the white tomb, and in its place he carved the name of Anne Catherick. The poor woman whom nobody had protected in life was at last remembered rightly in death. Walter laid flowers beneath the marble, and Laura stood beside him with bowed head, thinking of the frightened stranger who had warned her out of love, while Marian whispered that Mrs Fairlie would have been glad.

In the same little village church where Laura had once been married against her will, she was now married to the man she loved, on a bright and happy morning, and the whole village came to see. This time there was no cold dread in her face, only a calm and quiet joy, and when she answered her vows, her voice was clear. Marian stood at her side with tears running down her face, and did not even try to hide them.

In time a little son was born to Walter and Laura, and the whole household rejoiced as though a new light had been kindled in the house. Marian, who had so often been the protector of others, now found a new object for her devotion, and loved the baby as though he were her own, spending hours beside the cradle. The child had his mother's fair hair and his father's steady eyes, and the whole village agreed that he would grow up to be a fine man.

When Mr Fairlie, who had lived so long by avoiding every trouble, died at last in his shawl and his chair, his property passed by the old family arrangements to Laura's little son. The boy became the rightful heir of Limmeridge, and the great grey house, which had been so silent and fretful for so long, was filled once more with the noise of a happy family. Tenants and villagers cheered the news, for they remembered the day when his mother had come back among them.

Years later, on a warm summer night, Walter happened to walk along the very road where a hand had once touched his shoulder, and he stopped at the place where the pale stranger had asked him the way to London. He remembered her with gentleness and gratitude, for her warning had set in motion everything that followed, both the dark and the bright. Then he walked on toward home, with a quiet heart and a feeling that the circle was at last complete.

Walter set down the whole story in his own words, so that the truth about Laura might never again be doubted, and so that every person who had helped her might be remembered. It had begun on a lonely road beneath the moon, with a pale stranger and a few trembling words, and it ended in a house full of laughter. He laid down his pen and went out to join his family in the garden, where the evening light was falling softly on the grass.
